div.p: SCAMANDER.

Have you recognized, my boy, that these things are from Homer, or have you never recognized it at all, marvelling no doubt at how on earth fire could live in water? Let us, then, consider what it means; and look closely at the painting itself, only so far as to see those things from which the painting is drawn. You know, I suppose, the theme of the Iliad, in which Homer rouses Achilles over Patroclus, and the gods are moved to make war upon one another. Of all this that concerns the gods the painting knows nothing else, but it says that Hephaestus fell upon the Scamander in great and unmixed force. Look again: everything is from that source. This is the lofty city, and these the battlements of Ilium; this is a great plain, large enough to set Asia in array against Europe; this fire pours in flood across the plain, much of it creeping about the banks of the river, so that there are no longer any trees there. And the fire about Hephaestus streams over the water, and the river is in anguish and itself supplicates Hephaestus. Yet the river is not painted with hair, since it has been scorched all round, nor is Hephaestus lame, because he is running. And the bloom of the fire is not tawny, nor of the customary appearance, but gold-coloured and sun-coloured. These last things are no longer Homer's.
THE SINGING MAIDENS.

An Aphrodite of ivory, among soft myrtle-groves, is hymned by soft maidens. A teacher leads them, wise and not past her prime, for a certain bloom rests even upon a first wrinkle, drawing the stateliness of age yet mingling with it what is preserved of youthful vigour. The posture of the statue of Aphrodite is naked and graceful, and its material is a composition of close-grained ivory. But the goddess does not wish to seem to be painted; rather she stands out as if one might take hold of her. Will you have us pour a little speech as a libation upon the altar? For it has frankincense enough, and cassia and myrrh, and it seems to me to breathe also something of Sappho. The wisdom of the painting, then, must be praised: first, that in setting round the beloved stones he imitated them not from the colours but from the light, putting into them their transparency as a sharp point for the eye; next, that he allows us to hear the hymn too — for the maidens are singing, are singing, and the teacher glances askance at the one who sings out of tune, clapping her hands and bringing her sufficiently into the melody. As for their dress, it is simple and gives them no trouble if they should play — whether the girdle close to the skin, or the tunic at the arm, or how they delight in going barefoot, standing on the soft grass and drawing refreshment from the dew — and the meadow about their garments, and the colours in them, and how one suits one and another suits another, all this has been wonderfully imitated. For those who do not paint the accompanying details do not tell the truth in their paintings. As for the forms of the maidens, if we should entrust them to Paris or any other judge, he would, I think, be at a loss how to vote, so closely do they contend, rosy-armed and bright-eyed and fair-cheeked and honey-voiced — this last "the sweet address of Sappho." Love plays an accompaniment to them, having tilted back the curved arm of the bow, and the string sings full harmony and says it has all that the lyre has; and the eyes of the god are quick, conceiving, I think, some rhythm. What, then, do they sing? For something of the song too is painted. They say that Aphrodite was given forth from the sea by the effluence of Uranus, and at which of the islands she put in they do not yet say, but they will say Paphos, I think; and her birth they sing sufficiently. For by looking upward they show that she is from heaven, and by gently moving their upturned hands they make clear that she is from the sea, and their smile is a riddle of calm.
COMUS.

The spirit Comus, from whom comes men's revelry, stands at the doors of a bridal chamber — golden doors, I think, though they are slow to grasp because the scene is set as in night. Night is painted not from his body but from the occasion; and the porch shows that newly-wed and most prosperous people lie within the marriage-bed. And Comus has come, a young man among the young, soft and not yet a youth, flushed with wine and sleeping upright through drunkenness. He sleeps with his face thrown down upon his breast, showing nothing of his neck, and with his left hand resting on a hunting-spear; the hand, which seems to have held it, is relaxing and growing careless — the usual thing at the onset of sleep, when, as slumber coaxes us, reason passes into forgetfulness of the things it had been holding together; and so the little torch in his right hand seems to be slipping from his grasp, since sleep makes him heedless of it. Fearing the fire as it nears his leg, Comus swings his left shin over to the right and the torch over to the left, that he may turn aside the heat of the fire, drawing his hand away with the knee thrust out before it. Now faces are owed by painters to those in their prime, and without them paintings are blind; but for Comus little of his face is needed, since he bends down and draws over it the shadow from his head. He commands, I think, that those of his own age should not revel with faces uncovered. But the rest of the body is rendered in full detail, the little torch lighting it all round and bringing it into the light. The wreath of roses, let it be praised — yet not for its likeness, for to imitate the appearance of flowers with tawny and dark-blue colours, if it should so happen, is no great achievement — but one must praise the looseness of the wreath and its softness. I praise too the dewiness of the roses, and I say they have been painted together with their fragrance. What remains of Comus? What else than the revellers themselves? Do not the castanets strike upon you, and the resounding din, and the disordered song? Little torches gleam forth here and there, by which the revellers can both see what is at their feet and remain themselves unseen by us. Much laughter is roused as well, and the women rush along with the men, and put on sandals and gird themselves contrary to their nature; for revelry allows a woman to play the man and a man to slip on a woman's robe and walk like a woman. And the wreaths are no longer in bloom, but their gaiety has been taken from them by being fitted to the heads, because of the disorder of the running; for the freedom of the flowers refuses the hand, as one that withers them before their time. The painting imitates a certain clapping too, which revelry most requires, and the right hand, with its fingers curled in, strikes the hollow of the left held beneath it, so that the hands may sound in unison when struck, in the manner of cymbals.
THE EDUCATION OF ACHILLES.

Fawns and a hare — these are the game of the present Achilles; but the Achilles at Ilium will capture cities and horses and ranks of men, and the rivers will fight against him as he forbids them to flow; and for those deeds he will carry off as wages Briseis and the seven women from Lesbos, and gold and tripods, and the dependence of the Achaeans upon him; but these things here at Chiron's seem worth apples and honeycombs. And you are content, Achilles, with small gifts, you who will then disdain cities and the kinship of Agamemnon. The Achilles upon the trench, and he who routed the Trojans by his shout alone, and he who slays right and left and reddens the water of the Scamander, the immortal horses and the dragging of Hector and the man roaring over the breast of Patroclus — these Homer has painted; but he paints him also singing and praying and under one roof with Priam. This Achilles, however, does not yet understand valour, but is still a child; and Chiron, having nourished him on milk and marrow and honey, has given him to be painted soft and high-spirited and already nimble; for the boy's shin is straight, and his hands reach to his knee, since these are good escorts of running, and his hair is sweet and not unmoving, for Zephyr seems to play with it and rearrange it, so that, as it shifts this way and that, the boy seems now one, now another. There is already a frown and a spirited haughtiness upon the boy, but he softens it with a guileless eye and a most gracious cheek that casts a touch of tender laughter. The cloak he wears is, I think, his mother's, for it is beautiful and sea-purple and fire-bright, varying from being dark blue. Chiron coaxes him, as it were, to snatch up hares and to fly along with the fawns; at any rate, having just caught a fawn, he comes to Chiron and demands his prize, and Chiron rejoices to be asked, and crouching on his forefeet sets himself level with the boy, holding out to him from his bosom apples beautiful and fragrant — for the very fragrance of them seems painted in — and offers in his hand a honeycomb dripping a drop, by reason of the good order of the bees. For when, lighting on good pasture, they conceive, their combs grow full and their houses well over with honey. Chiron is painted in all respects a Centaur; but to join a horse to a man is no marvel, whereas to blend them and unite them, and, by Zeus, to make both leave off and begin together and elude the eyes should they try to detect where the human part ends, is the work, I think, of a good painter. And as for the gentleness that appears in Chiron's eye, it is wrought both by justice and by the prudence that comes from justice, but also by the lyre, by which he has been made musical; and now, too, there is something coaxing upon him, since Chiron knows that this soothes children and nourishes them more than milk does. These things are about the door of the cave; but the boy in the plain, playing horseman-fashion on the Centaur, is the same boy still. Chiron teaches Achilles to ride and to use him as one uses a horse, and measures out the gallop to what is bearable for the child; and when the boy laughs aloud from delight, he smiles back at him, turning round, and all but says: "See, I paw the ground for you, unwhipped; see, I urge you on too; the horse is swift, then, and takes away your fear. For having ridden me well, divine boy, and fit for such a horse, you shall one day be carried even by Xanthus and Balius, and you shall take many cities and slay many men, who, like you, will be like a god as they try in vain to flee." These things Chiron prophesies to the boy, beautiful and of good omen, and not such as Xanthus prophesied.
FABLES.

The fables resort to Aesop, loving him because he cares for them. For Homer too cared for fable, and Hesiod, and even Archilochus in his attack on Lycambes; but in Aesop all the affairs of men are made into fable, and he has given speech to the beasts for the sake of a moral. He checks greed and drives out insolence and deceit, and in this a lion plays a part for him, and a fox, and a horse, by Zeus, and not even the tortoise is voiceless — through whom children become learners of the business of life. The fables, then, in good repute thanks to Aesop, resort to the sage's doors to bind him with fillets and to crown him with a wreath of olive shoots. And he, I think, is weaving some fable. The smile on his face and his eyes fixed upon the ground show this; for the painter knows that the framing of fables requires a relaxed mind. The painting plays the philosopher too with the bodies of the fables, for, by bringing beasts together with men, it sets a chorus about Aesop, composed of the actors of his stage; and the fox is painted as leader of the chorus, since Aesop uses it as the minister of most of his plots, just as comedy uses Davus.
THE FEMALE CENTAURS.

You thought the herd of Centaurs sprang from oaks and rocks, or, by Zeus, from horses only, those upon which the son of Ixion is said to have begotten, from whom the Centaurs came into being mingled; but it seems they had mothers too of their own kind, and wives already, and foals in the shape of infants, and a most pleasant home. For I do not think you are vexed at Pelion and the life upon it, and the ash-tree, wind-nourished, which gives both straightness and the strength not to break at the spear-point, and the caves most beautiful, and the springs, and the female Centaurs beside them — like Naiads if we forget the horses, but, if we reckon them along with the horses, like Amazons; for the daintiness of the female form is given strength when the horse is seen joined to it. And these Centaur-infants — some lie in swaddling-clothes, some slip out of their swaddling-clothes, some seem to be crying, some thrive and smile as the breast flows well, some frolic beneath their mothers, some embrace them as they crouch, and one throws a stone at his mother, growing wanton already. The form of the babes is not yet clear, the milk so flooding them, but those already frisking show something of roughness too, and they have a mane just coming, and hooves still soft. How beautiful are the female Centaurs, even in the horse part! For some are grafted on white mares, some are joined to tawny ones, some are dappled, but they gleam like horses well groomed. And a white she-Centaur has sprung even from a black mare, and the most opposite of colours agree to the composition of beauty.
MENOECEUS.

This is the siege of Thebes, for the wall is seven-gated; the army is that of Polyneices son of Oedipus, for the companies are seven. Amphiaraus draws near them, downcast in look and understanding what they will suffer; and the other captains are afraid — and so they raise their hands to heaven — but Capaneus eyes the walls, scorning the battlements as captureable by a ladder. He is not yet, however, struck from the battlements, since the Thebans hesitate, I suppose, to begin the battle. Charming is the painter's device: enclosing the walls with armed men, he shows some of them whole, others indistinct as to their legs, others half-seen, the breasts only of some and the heads only, and helmets only, then spear-points. This is perspective, my boy. For the eyes must be deceived as they recede along with the proper foreshortenings. Nor is Thebes without its oracle, for Teiresias utters a certain prophecy bearing on Menoeceus, son of Creon — that if he should die where the dragon's lair was, the city would by this be set free. And he dies, unknown to his father, pitiable for his youth but blessed in his courage. For look at what the painter has done: he paints a youth not pale, nor bred in luxury, but spirited and breathing of the wrestling-ground, like the bloom of those honey-coloured boys whom the son of Ariston praises; and he frames him with a well-tinted breast and sides, and a well-proportioned haunch and thigh. He is strong, too, with the promise of his shoulders and a firm, unbending neck, and he has hair, only not too long. He stands over the dragon's lair, drawing out the sword that is already sunk in his side; and let us, my boy, receive his blood, holding out a fold of our garment for it, for it is pouring out, and his soul is already departing — and a little later you shall hear it cry out as it goes. For souls too have a love of beautiful bodies, and therefore they take leave of them unwillingly. As the blood drains slowly from him, he sinks down and welcomes death with a beautiful and tender eye, like one drawing on sleep.
HIPPOLYTUS.

The beast is the curse of Theseus, and it has fallen upon the horses of Hippolytus in the form of a grey-green bull, like the dolphins, and it comes from the sea against the youth with no justice at all; for his stepmother Phaedra, framing a charge against him that was not true — that he was, forsooth, loved by Hippolytus, whereas she herself loved the youth — Theseus is deceived by the tale and curses his son, and these are the things you see. The horses, you observe, having dishonoured the yoke, raise their manes free, nor do they paw the ground like the splendid and sensible ones, but are lifted up with fear and panic, and, sprinkling the plain with foam, one has turned toward the beast in flight, one has reared up against it, one looks askance, while for one the rush is toward the sea, as if he had forgotten both himself and the land, and with nostrils erect they neigh shrilly — unless you misread the painting. As for the wheels of the chariot, one has had its spokes wrenched off by the chariot's leaning against it, while the other, having left the axle, is carried along by itself, the whirl still spinning it. The horses of the attendants too are panic-stricken, and some they throw off, others, already strangling them, they drag along. But you, youth, in love with chastity, suffered unjust things at the hands of your stepmother, and more unjust at the hands of your father, so that the painting too has lamented, composing a kind of poetic dirge over you. For these crags, on which you hunted with Artemis, tear their cheeks in the form of women; the meadows in the bloom of youths, which you used to call inviolate, wither their flowers over you; and the Nymphs, your nurses, rising up from these springs, rend their hair and pour out water from their breasts. Neither did your manliness avail you anything, nor your arm; rather, some of your limbs are torn, others crushed, and your hair is fouled, and your breast is still breathing, as if it would not let go the soul, while the eye gazes round upon the wounds. Alas for your beauty, how it had escaped notice as being invulnerable! For not even now does it abandon the youth, but something of it shines even upon the wounds.
THE CUBITS.

About the Nile the Cubits sport, children matched to the name; and the Nile rejoices in them above measure, both for other reasons and because they proclaim how great he has flooded forth for the Egyptians. They are brought to him, and as it were they come to him out of the water, soft and smiling infants, and they have, I think, something of the talkative in them too; some sit on his shoulders, some hang from his locks, some sleep in the crook of his arm, some revel upon his breast. And he gives them up flowers, some from his bosom, some from his arm, that they may both weave wreaths from them and sleep, holy and fragrant, upon the flowers; and the children climb one upon another, with rattles too, for these are native to that water. Now the crocodiles and the river-horses, which some add to the Nile in their pictures, lie hidden in the deep eddy, lest fear should fall upon the children. And tokens of farming and of seafaring reveal the Nile by the following reasoning, my boy: the Nile, having made Egypt navigable, then gives it, drunk dry by the plains, the use of fruitful soil. In Ethiopia, where he begins, a spirit who is his steward stands over him, by whom he is sent forth in season, measured to the times. He is painted as tall enough to be conceived as reaching to the sky, and he holds his foot upon the springs, inclining toward them, like Poseidon himself. To this spirit the river looks, and asks that his infants may be many.
RHODOGUNE.

The blood, upon the bronze and the scarlet cloaks, casts a certain bloom upon the army; and there is grace in the painting — the horses fallen in different attitudes, and others disordered in their terror, and the river-water spoiled and corrupted, beside which all this is, and the captives, and the trophy raised over them. Rhodogune and the Persians defeat the Armenians, who had broken the truce; whereupon Rhodogune is said to have won the battle without allowing herself even so much delay as to gather up the right side of her hair. Is she not lifted up and proud of the victory, and aware that she will be sung of for the deed, both on the lyre and on the pipe and wherever there are Greeks? Beside her too is painted a Nisaean mare, black upon white legs, with white breast and breath from a white nostril and a forehead in a perfect circle. Now of stones and necklaces and all soft adornment Rhodogune has yielded to the mare, that she may glory and daintily champ her bit; but Rhodogune herself shines forth in all things, except in her own beauty, with a scarlet-dyed robe, in a pretty girdle that measures the robe to the knee, and pretty trousers showing patterns from the loom. From shoulder to elbow brooches join the tunic where it parts, the forearm showing through at the intervals where the fastening is; and the shoulder is set, and the posture is not yet that of an Amazon. One must admire too the shield's moderate size, sufficient for the breast, and examine here the strength of the painting; for the left hand, reaching beyond the handgrip, holds the spear, keeping the shield away from the breast, and, since the rim stands out straight, even the outside of the shield is seen — are not these parts golden, and like living creatures? — while the inside, where the hand is, is sea-purple, and the forearm blooms beside it. You seem to me, my boy, to perceive the beauty in her, and to wish to hear something about this too. Listen, then. She is pouring a libation over the rout of the Armenians, and her thought is that of one praying. And she prays to capture the men whom she has now captured, for she does not seem to me to love being loved. The part of her hair that is bound up is adorned with modesty, which chastens her high spirit, while the loose part fills her with Bacchic frenzy and gives her strength; and the disordered hair is tawny and beyond gold, while the part lying on the other side has something that shifts into a gleam by reason of being arranged. Of her eyebrows it is charming that they begin from the same point and spring up together from the nose, more charming still that they are arched; for they must not only be set out before the eyes but also be set round them. The cheek receives the longing that comes from the eyes, and gives delight by its cheerfulness, for the love of smiles is most of all in the cheek; and the eyes are blended from bright to dark, and give cheerfulness from the occasion, beauty from nature, and pride from command. The mouth is soft and full of erotic fruit, most sweet to kiss but not easy to describe; yet, of what is enough for you to learn, look, my child: lips flowery and even, a mouth well-proportioned and uttering the prayer to the trophy — and if we should wish to overhear it, perhaps it will speak Greek.
THE LOVES.

The Loves, see, are gathering apples; and if their number is great, do not be amazed — for they become children of nymphs and govern all that is mortal, many for the many things that men desire; but the heavenly Love, they say, attends in heaven to things divine. Have you perhaps caught some of the fragrance about the garden, or are you slow to it? Listen eagerly, for along with the discourse the very apples will strike upon you. These are rows of trees set upright in order, with freedom to walk down the middle of them. A soft grass covers the paths, soft enough to be a couch for one who lies down. From the tips of the boughs apples golden and ruddy and sun-coloured invite the whole swarm of the Loves to harvest them. Now here are quivers, gold-studded and golden, and the arrows within them; but the whole flock is stripped of these, and they fly about light, having hung their arrows on the apple-trees. Their embroidered cloaks lie on the grass, and the flowers on them are countless. Nor are their heads wreathed, since their own hair suffices them. Their wings — dark-blue and crimson and golden in some — all but strike the very air with a musical harmony. Ah, the baskets into which they put the apples — how much sard is about them, how much emerald, how genuine the pearl! Their making must be conceived as Hephaestus' own. Nor do they need ladders to the trees from him, for high up, even to the apples themselves, they fly. And — not to speak of those who dance, or run to and fro, or sleep, or how they rejoice when they have eaten of the apples — let us see what these four here are about. For the most beautiful of the Loves, see, four of them, have withdrawn from the rest: two of them are tossing an apple back and forth to each other, and of the second pair one shoots at the other and the other shoots back, and there is no threat upon their faces; rather, they offer their breasts to each other, that the arrows may lodge there. The riddle is beautiful: consider, then, whether I understand anything of the painter. This is friendship, my boy, and longing for each other; for the pair playing with the apple are beginning desire, whence the one lets it fly after kissing it, and the other receives it with upturned hands, plainly to kiss it in return if he catches it, and to send it back again; while the pair of archers confirm a love that is already established. And I say that the one pair are playing at the beginning of loving, the others shooting that their longing may not cease. But those others, round whom the throng of spectators stand, have fallen together in anger, and a kind of wrestling holds them. Let me describe the wrestling too, since you press for it: the one has caught his opponent, flying down upon his back, and grips him in a stranglehold and binds him fast with his legs; the other neither gives up, but rises upright and breaks the hand by which he is being throttled, by twisting one of its fingers, after which the rest no longer have hold nor are clenched tight; and the one being twisted is in pain and bites the wrestler's ear. So the watching Loves are vexed with him as a wrongdoer who fouls in wrestling, and pelt him with apples. And let not that hare there escape us; let us hunt it down along with the Loves. This animal, crouching beneath the apple-trees and feeding on the apples that fall to the ground, leaving many half-eaten, these Loves hunt and harry — one with a clapping of hands, one shouting, one shaking his cloak; and some fly over the creature crying out, others pursue it on foot upon the track, one has rushed as if to fling himself upon it and the creature has turned another way, one plots against the hare's leg, and another it has slipped from after he had caught it. So they laugh and have fallen down, one on his side, one face-forward, others on their backs, all in the postures of failure. But no one shoots; rather they try to take it alive, as a most welcome offering to Aphrodite. For you know, I suppose, what is said about the hare, that much of Aphrodite belongs to it; it is said indeed to suckle the young it has borne and to give birth again upon the same milk, and to conceive afresh, and no time is empty for it of bringing forth; and the male begets, as is the nature of males, and also conceives, contrary to its nature. But absurd lovers have found in it even a kind of erotic persuasion, hunting their beloved by forcible craft. Let us, then, leave such things to unjust men, unworthy of being loved in return; but do you look at Aphrodite for me. Where, then, and at what part of the orchard is she? Do you see the overhanging rock, from beneath which there runs out a stream most dark-blue, fresh and fit to drink, which is also channelled off to be drink for the apple-trees? There conceive Aphrodite for me, the nymphs, I think, having set her up because she made them mothers of the Loves and therefore blessed in children. And the silver mirror, and that gilded sandal, and the golden brooches — all these hang there not idly; they declare that they are Aphrodite's, and this is written there, and they are said to be gifts of the nymphs; and the Loves offer first-fruits of the apples and stand round praying that the orchard may be beautiful for them.
ARRHICHION.

You have come to Olympia itself, and to the most beautiful of the things at Olympia; for this is the men's pancratium, and Arrhichion is crowned for it, having died upon the victory; and this man, a Hellanodikes, crowns him — let him be addressed as "the just," both because he is careful of the truth and because he is painted, as those are. The land provides a stadium in a soft valley running inward just so far; and the stream of the Alpheus issues forth light — and so it alone of rivers runs upon the sea — and wild-olive trees have blossomed beside it, of grey-green hue, beautiful and like the curling of parsley. These, then, we shall examine after the stadium, and many other things; but let us look at the deed of Arrhichion before it has ceased, for he seems to have conquered not only his adversary but the Greek people too. At any rate, they spring up from their seats and shout, and some shake their hands, some their garments, some leap up from the ground, some gladly wrestle with those near them; for things so astounding do not allow the spectators to remain in self-command. Or who is so insensible as not to cry out at the athlete? For, great as it already was for him to have won the Olympic crown twice, greater is this now, when, having won it at the cost of his very soul, he is sent to the place of the blessed with the dust still upon him. And let no one think this a chance, for the wrestling-trick of victory was most wisely contrived. Those who practise the pancratium, my boy, use a perilous kind of wrestling, for they must throw themselves on their backs, which is not safe for a wrestler, and use grips in which one must win by seeming to fall; and they need skill to strangle now in one way, now in another; the same men wrestle with the ankle and twist the hand, with the addition of striking and leaping upon their opponent — for these are the works of the pancratium, except for biting and gouging. The Lacedaemonians, indeed, permit even these, training themselves, I suppose, for battle; but the Eleans and the games exclude them, while they approve of strangling. Whence the adversary, having already caught Arrhichion about the waist, resolved to kill him, and thrust his forearm against his throat, cutting off his breath, and, fitting his legs against the groin and twining the tips of his feet about each of Arrhichion's knees, he got the start of him with the stranglehold, the sleep of the death thereupon already running over his senses. But, having relaxed the pressure of his legs, he failed to anticipate the cunning of Arrhichion; for Arrhichion, kicking away the sole of the foot by which his right side was endangered, the hollow of the knee being already loosened, holds his opponent fast by the groin so that he is no longer an adversary, and, sinking down upon his left side and locking the tip of the foot within the bend of the knee, by a violent outward wrench does not let the ankle-bone stay in its socket; for the soul, as it departs from the body, makes it feeble, yet gives it strength for what it presses upon. Now the man who strangled is painted like a corpse, signalling his surrender with his hand; but Arrhichion is painted as victors are, for the blood is in its bloom and the sweat still fresh, and he smiles, as the living do when they perceive victory.
MEMNON.

This is the army of Memnon; their arms are laid aside, and they lay out the greatest of their number for lamentation — struck, it seems to me, in the breast by the ash-spear. For finding a broad plain, and tents, and a wall within a camp, and a city fenced about with walls, I cannot see how these are not Ethiopians and this not Troy; and Memnon, son of the Dawn, is being mourned. Him, when he came to defend Troy, the son of Peleus slew, they say — though he came great and in no way smaller than Achilles. For consider how great he lies upon the ground, and how great the harvest of his curls, which, I think, the Nile nourished; for the Egyptians have the mouths of the Nile, but the Ethiopians its springs. Look at his form, how strong it is even though his eyes are lost; look at the down on his cheek, how it matches in age his slayer. Nor would you call Memnon black, for the unmixed black in him shows a kind of bloom. The spirits aloft — Dawn, mourning over her child, makes the Sun downcast and begs Night to come before the time and to hold back the camp, that it may be granted her to steal away her son, Zeus, I suppose, having so nodded his assent. And see, he has been stolen away and is at the very edge of the painting. Nowhere is there a tomb of Memnon; but Memnon is in Ethiopia, transformed into black stone, and the figure is that of one seated, though the form, I think, is his own; and the ray of the Sun strikes upon the statue, for the Sun seems, like a plectrum falling on the mouth, to call forth a voice from Memnon and by this clever device to console the Day with words.
ANTILOCHUS.

That Achilles loved Antilochus you have detected, I think, in Homer, seeing that Antilochus is the youngest of the Greeks, and considering the half-talent of gold set for the contest; and he reports to Achilles that Patroclus lies dead, Menelaus having devised a comfort along with the message, in that Achilles turned his eyes upon his beloved; and he mourns for the beloved in his grief, and clasps his hands, lest he kill himself; and Achilles, I think, rejoices both at his touch and at his weeping. These, then, are Homer's paintings; but here is the painter's drama. Memnon, coming from Ethiopia, slays Antilochus as he shields his father, and strikes terror into the Achaeans like a thing of dread, for before Memnon the black men are a fable. But the Achaeans, prevailing over the body, lament Antilochus — the sons of Atreus, and the man from Ithaca, and the son of Tydeus, and the namesakes; and the Ithacan is distinguished by his sternness and wakefulness, Menelaus by his gentleness, Agamemnon by his inspired look, and the son of Tydeus the painter shows by his frankness; you would recognize the son of Telamon too by his grimness, and the Locrian by his readiness. And the army mourns the youth, standing about him in a dirge, and, having fixed their spears in the ground, they cross their feet and lean upon the spears, propping their heads, heavy with grief, most of them. Achilles is to be shown not by his hair, for that is gone from him after Patroclus, but by his form and his stature and the very fact that he no longer wears his hair long. He mourns, lying upon the breast of Antilochus, and promises, I think, a pyre and what is for it, and his armour perhaps, and the head of Memnon; for he will make Memnon pay as much as Hector, that in this too Antilochus may have no less than Patroclus. And Memnon, in the army of the Ethiopians, stands terrible, holding a spear, with a lion-skin fastened about him, and grinning at Achilles. Let us consider Antilochus too: he is coming to manhood, his cheek down-covered, and wears his sun-bleached hair long. Light is his shin, and his body well-proportioned for ease of running, and the blood has bloomed like a colour upon ivory, the spear having entered his breast. The youth lies, not downcast, nor to be likened to a corpse, but bright and smiling; for the joy of having saved his father, carried in his face, Antilochus, I think, kept even as he perished by the spear, and the soul left his face not as he was in pain, but as the joyful part prevailed.
AMYMONE.

You have met Poseidon, I think, in Homer, walking over the sea, when he sets out from Aegae against the Achaeans, and the sea keeps calm, escorting him with his very horses and his very sea-monsters, for those too follow and fawn on Poseidon, as here. There, then, you are aware of mainland horses, since the poet thinks fit that they be bronze-footed and swift-flying and struck by the whip; but here the chariot is drawn by hippocamps, web-footed and swimming and grey-eyed, and, by Zeus, like dolphins. And there Poseidon seems vexed and indignant with Zeus for inclining the balance toward the Greeks and judging in their favour from the worse cause; but here he is painted bright, and looks cheerful, and is in a great erotic flutter. For Amymone, daughter of Danaus, frequenting the water of Inachus, has overcome the god, and he sets out to hunt her, though she does not yet understand that she is loved. The terror of the maiden, indeed, and her trembling, and the golden pitcher slipping from her hands, show that Amymone is struck with amazement and at a loss as to what Poseidon means by abandoning the sea altogether; and upon her, white as she is by nature, the gold sheds a gleam, mingling its brightness with the water. Let us give way, my boy, to the nymph, for already a wave is curving toward the marriage; the wave is still grey and of the bright colour, but Poseidon will paint it purple.
MELES.

The story of the Enipeus, and how Tyro loved the water, has been told by Homer, who tells also of the deceit by Poseidon and the bloom of the wave, beneath which was the bridal bed; but this story is another, not from Thessaly but Ionian. Cretheis in Ionia loves the Meles, and he is like a young man and is seen by the spectator whole, casting himself out there from where he begins. She drinks though not thirsty, and lays hold of the water, and converses with its murmur as if it were talking, and sheds erotic tears into the water, and the river — for it loves in return — rejoices in their mingling. Charming, then, in the painting, is the Meles himself, lying among crocus and lotus, and rejoicing in the hyacinth for the youthfulness of the flower, and presenting a form dainty and youthful and not unwise — you would say that the eyes of the Meles are pondering something of poetry. And charming too is it in him that he does not give forth his springs in a violent rush, as it is the custom to paint the boorish rivers, but, scratching the earth with the tips of his fingers, he holds his hand to the water as it bubbles up noiselessly; and he appears to us, as he did to Cretheis, to be water, and she sits beside a dream, they say. But these are no dream, Cretheis, nor do you draw this love upon water; for the river loves you, I know well, and contrives for you a bridal chamber, raising a wave beneath which the bed will be. And if you disbelieve, I will tell you the artifice of the chamber too: a slender breeze, running beneath the wave, makes it curved and enclosing and still in bloom, for the reflected light of the sun casts a colour upon the lifted water. Why, then, my boy, do you lay hold of me? Why do you not let me go through the rest of the painting too? If you wish, let us describe Cretheis as well, since you say you rejoice whenever the discourse plays among them. Let it be said, then: her form is dainty and very Ionian, and modesty becomes the form, and this bloom is enough for the cheek; her hair is gathered up beneath the ear, and is adorned besides with a sea-purple veil. The veil, I think, is a gift of a Nereid or a Naiad, for it is likely that the goddesses joined the dance over the Meles, who provides his springs not far from the mouth. She looks so sweet and simple that not even her tears alter her graciousness, and her neck is sweeter still for not being adorned; for necklaces and the gleam of stones and collars are not unpleasingly added to women of moderate beauty, and, by Zeus, lend them something of charm, but they work against the ugly and the over-beautiful, the one being exposed by them, the other led away from. Let us examine her hands: soft are the fingers and well-grown and white as far as the forearm; and you see the forearm too, how it shows whiter through the white garment, and the upright breasts gleam. Why, then, are the Muses here? And why upon the springs of the Meles? When the Athenians were colonizing Ionia, the Muses led the fleet in the form of bees, for they delighted in Ionia because of the Meles, as more potable than Cephisus and Olmeius. You will meet them here once dancing, then; but now the Muses are spinning the birth of Homer, since it pleases the Fates; and the Meles, through the boy, will grant that Peneus be silver-eddying, that Titaresius be light and easy-flowing, that Enipeus be divine and Axius most beautiful, and will grant to Xanthus his descent from Zeus and to Ocean that all are descended from him.
THE MARSH.

The land is sodden with rain, and bears reeds and rushes, which the natural richness of marshes gives unsown and unploughed; and tamarisk too is painted, and galingale, for these also belong to the marshes. Mountains tall enough to reach the sky are set round about, of no single nature: those that put forth the pine declare the soil thin, those that flourish with cypress speak of clayey ground, while those firs — what else than that the mountain is wintry and rugged? For they do not welcome the clod, nor do they love to be warmed; and so for that very reason they dwell apart from the plains, since they grow more easily on the mountains. Springs gush from the mountains, which, flowing down and pooling their water, make the plain a marsh — not, however, a disorderly one, nor as it were a tangle: its stream has been led through it by the painting, just as nature, the wisest of all, would have led it, and it winds in many meanders, abounding in parsley, good for the water-birds to sail upon. For you see, no doubt, the ducks, how, web-footed, they glide along, blowing up little jets, as it were pipes, of water. And what of the tribe of geese? They too are painted according to their nature, floating on the surface and swimming. And those on tall legs, with their over-long beaks, you perceive, I think, to be foreign, and dainty, each in a different plumage; and their attitudes too are various. For one rests its two feet upon a rock, one by one; another cools its wing; another preens; another has caught something out of the water; another has bent down to the land to take in some food from there. That the swans should be driven by the Loves is no wonder, for the gods are wanton and clever at sporting with birds; so let us not pass over their charioteering idly, nor the very water in which all this is. For this water is the most beautiful part of the marsh, the land providing it from its own depths, and it gathers into a beautiful swimming-pool. For through the middle of the water unfading plants lean, some this way, some that, sweet ears of grain pelting the water with their bloom. About these the Loves drive their birds, holy and golden-bridled — one giving the bird full rein, one checking it, one turning it about, one driving it round the turning-post — and you may suppose them to be heard urging on the swans, and threatening one another and jeering, for this is upon their faces; and one throws down his neighbour, one has thrown another down, one is content to fall from his bird, that he may bathe in the race-course. And round about, on the banks, stand the more musical of the swans, singing, I think, the high-pitched strain, as befits the competitors. Do you see the winged boy? This is the wind Zephyr, giving the song to the swans. He is painted soft and graceful, as a riddle of the breeze, and the swans have spread their wings to be struck by the wind. See, a river too steals out of the marsh, broad and gently swelling; and goatherds and shepherds cross it on a bridge. Now if you should praise the painter for the goats, that he has painted them frisking and high-spirited, or the sheep, that their gait is leisurely and their fleeces like a burden, or if we should go through the pipes, or those who use them, how they pipe with lips drawn in, we shall praise but a little of the painting, and only so far as imitation goes; but we shall not praise its wisdom, nor its timeliness, which are thought the best things of the art. What, then, is the wisdom? He has thrown a bridge of palm-trees across the river, and a most pleasant tale along with it. For knowing what is said about palms, that one of them is male, the other female, and having heard about their marriage, that they wed the females by enfolding them with their branches and straining themselves toward them, one of each kind set on either bank, he has painted it; and so the male is in love and leans over and arches across the river, but, since the female still stands apart and he cannot reach her, he lies down and is enslaved, having bridged the water, and is safe for those who cross by reason of the roughness of his bark.
PANTHEIA.

The fair Pantheia is painted by Xenophon in respect of her character — that she rejected Araspas, and was not overcome by Cyrus, and wished to draw a common grave to Abradatas; but what her hair was like, and how great her eyebrow, and how she looked, and how it was with her mouth, Xenophon has not yet said, clever though he is at chattering about such things. But a man not competent to write history, yet most competent to paint, who never met Pantheia herself but conversed with Xenophon, paints Pantheia such as he inferred her to be in soul. The walls, my boy, and the burning houses and the beautiful Lydian women — let us leave it to the Persians to carry off and capture whatever of these is captureable. And Croesus, on whom the pyre is, does not concern Xenophon himself; for he does not acknowledge it, or else concedes it to Cyrus. But Abradatas, and Pantheia who died over him, since the painting wills it, let us consider — what a drama it is. These two loved each other, and the woman made her own adornment armour for him; and he was fighting for Cyrus against Croesus on a four-poled chariot and eight horses, still young, with soft down on his cheek, at the season when the poets too think the trees pitiable when they are cast out of the earth. The wounds, my boy, are such as from sabre-bearers, for cutting down is suitable to such a battle; and the blood being fresh, part stains the armour, part himself, and there is some that is sprinkled on the crest, while the plume, hyacinthine, rises from the golden helmet, flashing upon the very gold. Beautiful, then, are these arms as a shroud, at least for one who did not disgrace them nor cast them away in battle; and Cyrus brings many Assyrian and Lydian gifts to the brave man, among others golden sand upon a wagon from the idle treasuries of Croesus; but Pantheia does not think the tomb has its fitting things, unless she herself become a shroud for Abradatas. The dagger, indeed, she has already driven through her breast, but so very firmly that she does not even break out into a wail over it. She lies, at any rate, her mouth keeping its own proportion and, by Zeus, its bloom, whose flower is so upon her lips that it shines forth even while she is silent. She has not yet drawn out the dagger, but still drives it in, holding it by the hilt — and the hilt is likened to a golden club with emeralds for its knobs. But sweeter are the fingers — and her form is in no way altered by pain, for she does not even seem to be in pain, but to depart rejoicing, because she sends herself away; and she departs not, like the wife of Protesilaus, crowned with the things in which she had revelled, nor, like the wife of Capaneus, lifted up as if for sacrifice, but, her beauty unadorned and such as it was in the time of Abradatas, she keeps it and carries it away, pouring her hair, not yet black and abundant, about her shoulders and neck, and showing a white throat which she has torn, yet not so as to disfigure it, for the marks of the nails are sweeter than the painting. The redness on the cheek does not desert her even in death, and the providers of it are her bloom and her modesty. See too the nostrils, drawn up in moderation and making a base for the nose, from which, like crescent-shaped shoots, the eyebrows spring up, black beneath the white forehead. But the eyes, my boy, let us not regard for their size, nor because they are dark, but let us consider the intelligence that is in them, and, by Zeus, how much of the soul's good things they drew in — disposed pitiably, yet not divorced from cheerfulness; courageous, yet more within the bounds of reason than of daring; comprehending death, yet not yet departing. And longing, the attendant of love, is so poured over the eyes that it most plainly drips from them. Love too is painted in the history of the deed, and so is Lydia, receiving the blood, and in a golden lap, as you see.
AMPHION.

The device of the lyre Hermes is said to have first fixed together out of two horns and a crossbar and a tortoise-shell, and to have given the gift, after Apollo and the Muses, to Amphion the Theban; and he, dwelling at Thebes when it was not yet walled, sent forth strains upon the stones, and the stones, hearing, ran together. For these are the things in the painting. First, then, study the lyre, whether it is painted true to itself. The horn is from a leaping goat, the poets say; the musician uses it for the lyre, the archer for his own purposes. You see the horns are black and notched, and dreadful to gore with; and the wood, of all that the lyre needs, is all of boxwood, hard and smooth in its grain. There is no ivory anywhere in the lyre, since men did not yet know either the beast itself or what use they would make of its horns. The tortoise-shell is black, but rendered accurate to nature, and is encircled with hollow rings, joined one to another, with tawny bosses; the strings, on the part toward the bridge, lie exposed and meet the bosses, while toward the crossbar they appear hollow. This posture of theirs is most proportionate, that they should recline upright on the lyre. And what does Amphion say? What else than that he plays and bends his mind to the harp and shows a little of his teeth, as much as is enough for a singer? He sings, I think, of the Earth, that, being the begetter and mother of all things, she now gives walls of her own accord. His hair is sweet even of itself, straying over his forehead, descending with the down beside his ear, and showing a touch of gold — sweeter still with the headband, which the poets of secret matters say the Graces made, a most pleasant ornament and most suited to the lyre. I fancy that Hermes, caught by love, gave both gifts to Amphion. And the cloak he wears, that too is perhaps from Hermes; for it does not stay one colour, but shifts and varies its bloom like the rainbow. He sits on a mound, beating time with his foot, and with his right hand striking the strings he plays, while the other hand is held with the fingers straight outstretched — which I had thought only modelling could boldly do. Well then, how is it with the stones? They all run together toward the song and listen and become a wall; and part of it is built up, part is rising, part they have just reached. The stones are eager and glad and serve their apprenticeship to music; and the wall is seven-gated, as many as are the notes of the lyre.
CASSANDRA.

Those lying here and there about the men's hall, and the blood mingled with the wine, and those breathing their last upon the tables, and this mixing-bowl kicked over by a man who writhes beside it, and the prophesying maiden in her gown, looking at the axe about to fall upon her — Agamemnon, come from Troy, Clytemnestra receives in this fashion; and the rest are slain, some by some, drunk as they are, so that even Aegisthus took courage for the deed. Clytemnestra, having enveloped Agamemnon by the device of a robe with no outlet, brought down upon him this double-edged axe, which fells even great trees; and the daughter of Priam, judged most beautiful, singing for Agamemnon her disbelieved prophecies, she slays with the hot axe. And if we examine these things as a drama, my boy, great matters have been put on the stage in little; but if as a painting, you will see more in them. For look: these lamps are the providers of light, since this is by night; those mixing-bowls are the providers of drink — the golden ones brighter than the fire; and the tables are full of meats, the meats of kings on which the heroes feasted, but none of these is in order, for, as the banqueters die, some are kicked over, some crushed, some lie fallen from them; and cups fall from the hands, most of them full of gore; and there is no defence in the dying, for they are drunk. As for the attitudes of those lying there: one has his throat cut as it drew in food or drink; one has his head cut off as he stooped over the mixing-bowl; one has had the hand struck off that carried a cup; one drags the table with him as he falls from the couch; one lies upon his shoulders and head — a poet would say "head-foremost"; one disbelieves the death; one has not the strength to flee, as if drunkenness were a fetter cast upon him; and none of those lying there is pale, since the bloom does not at once desert those who die in wine. But the most sovereign part of the scene Agamemnon holds, lying not in the Trojan plains, nor on any shores of the Scamander, but among youths and women, an ox at the manger — for this is what comes after toils and at the banquet. More sovereign in pity, however, is the part of Cassandra: how Clytemnestra stands over her with the axe, looking madly and with hair flung wild and a savage forearm, while Cassandra herself, in a daintily and inspired state, has set herself to fall upon Agamemnon, casting from her the fillets and as it were embracing him by her art; but, the axe being already raised, she turns her eyes there, and cries out so pitiably that even Agamemnon, with the remnant of his soul, pities her as he hears this — for he will remember it even in Hades, before Odysseus, in the assembly of the souls.
PHAETHON.

Golden are the tears of the Heliades; the story is that they flow for Phaethon. For he, having been born a son of Helios, dared his father's chariot in his desire for charioteering, and, not keeping hold of the reins, was thrown and fell into the Eridanus. To the wise these things seem to be a kind of excess of the fiery element, but to poets and painters they are horses and a chariot, and the heavens are thrown into confusion. For look: Night drives the Day from the meridian, and the disc of the sun, streaming earthward, draws the stars after it. The Hours, abandoning the gates, flee into the gloom that meets them, and the horses, having fallen out of the yoke, are carried away in frenzy; the Earth refuses and lifts her hands aloft, as the raging fire comes upon her. And the youth falls and is carried downward, for his hair is set ablaze and his breast smoulders, and he is about to fall into the river Eridanus and to furnish a kind of legend to the water; for swans, blowing up sweet notes thereafter, will make a song of the youth, and flocks of them, raised over the Caÿster and the Ister, will sing these things, and nothing will be unaware of such a story; and they will use Zephyr, light and a fellow-traveller, for the song, for he is said to have agreed to join the swans in their dirge. These things, too, are present to the birds, so that it is time for them to make music like instruments. And the women on the bank, who are not yet trees — they say the Heliades, over their brother, were transformed and ended as trees, and that they let fall tears. The painting knows this too: for these, casting roots from their ankles, are trees as far as the navel, and the boughs already overtake their hands. Ah, their hair, how it has all become poplar! Ah, their tears, how golden! And the tear that floods in the socket of the eyes shines upon the bright pupils and draws, as it were, a ray; the one that meets the cheeks glistens around its ruddiness; while those dripping down the breast are gold already. The river too mourns, raising himself out of his eddy, and holds out a fold to Phaethon, for he has received the colour; and he will soon farm the Heliades, for with the breezes and frosts that he sends up he will work them into stone and will receive them when they fall, and through his bright water will carry off to the barbarians on the Ocean the splinters of the poplars.
PAN.

The Nymphs say that Pan dances badly and leaps beyond what is fitting, lifting himself up and springing aloft like the wanton goats, and that they would teach him another dance, sweeter in manner; but he pays no heed to them, and as he tries them and lays hold of their bosoms they set upon him at midday, when Pan is said to sleep, having quit the hunt. Now formerly he used to sleep relaxed and gentle of nose, soothing its irascibility with sleep; but today he is over-wrathful, for the Nymphs, having fallen upon him, have already pulled his hands behind him, and he fears for his legs, since they wish to seize them. As for his beard, of which he makes most account, it has been shaved off, knives having been set to it; and they say they will persuade Echo too to despise him and to utter no sound to him any more. These things the Nymphs do all together; but do you look at them by their several tribes. For the forms of the Naiads sprinkle drops from their hair; the dryness about the cowherd-Nymphs is no worse than dew; and those that are in flower have hair growing like hyacinthine flowers.
THE BOSPORUS.

. . . they cry out, and they seem to encourage the horses too not to throw the children, nor to spit out the bit, but to take and trample down the beasts; and the horses, I think, hear and do these things. When they have hunted and taken their feast, a ship ferries them from Europe to Asia, about four stades — for this is the distance between the two continents — and they sail as their own rowers. See, they cast their mooring-line, and there receives them a most pleasant house, showing chambers and men's halls and the traces of windows; and a wall is thrown round it and has battlements. Its most beautiful feature is a semicircular portico, tawny-coloured from the stone in it. The stone has its origin from springs, for a hot stream, flowing out beneath the mountains of lower Phrygia and led into the quarries, makes some of the rocks soaked with rain and gives a watery growth to the stones, whence their many colours: where it stagnates it gives a muddy and tawny tinge, where it is clear, there it gives a crystalline one, and it dapples the rocks, soaking through their many openings. The shore is high and bears tokens of such a tale as this: a girl and a boy, both beautiful, frequenting the same teacher, were inflamed with love for each other, and, since there was no liberty to embrace, set out to die from this very rock, and from here were borne into the sea in their last and their first embraces; and Love, upon the rock, stretches out his hand toward the sea, the painter hinting at the tale. The next house: a widowed woman lives there, having left the city because of the throng of young men, for they said they would carry her off and reveled without restraint and tried her with gifts; and she, I think, having some neat way with them, teases the youths and, having slipped away here, dwells in this fortified house. For consider how it is fortified: a cliff stands over the sea, undermined at the parts washed by the waves, while at the top it juts out and supports this seaside house, by reason of which the sea too appears more dark-blue, when the eyes are cast down into it; and the land furnishes everything that a ship has, except motion. Even when she has come to this stronghold her lovers have not for all that abandoned her, but one in a dark-prowed, one in a gilt-prowed, another in some other of the gay little boats, sails up; and the revel itself is of handsome men, garlanded, and one pipes, one says he is clapping, one sings, I think, and they toss up wreaths and kisses, and they do not even row but hold their oars and lie at anchor under the cliff. And the woman from the house, as from a watch-tower, sees all this and laughs at the revel, growing wanton toward her lovers, as one who forces them not only to sail but even to swim. And as you go on you will meet with flocks, and will hear lowing cattle, and the sound of pipes will ring about you, and you will meet with huntsmen and farmers and rivers and lakes and springs — for the painting has imprinted both the things that are and the things that come to be, and how some things might come to be, not playing false with the truth on account of their multitude, but accomplishing what is proper to each, as if it were painting one thing only — until we come to Hieron. And there, I think, you see the temple, and the pillars set round it, and the beacon at the mouth, which is hung up for the fire-signalling of the ships that sail out of the Pontus.

Why, then, do you not lead me on to something else? For I have considered the Bosporus enough. What will you say? The matter of the fishermen has escaped me, which I promised at the beginning. So, that we may not go through small things but those worth speaking of, let us leave out of the account those who hunt with the rod, or contrive with the weel, or whoever hauls up a net or drives in a trident — for you will hear little about them, and they will seem to you rather seasonings of the painting — and let us look at those who attack the tunny, for these are worth speaking of for the greatness of the catch. The tunny resort to the outer sea, having had their birth and their pastures in the Pontus, some of fishes, some of mud and other juices which the Ister and the Maeotis bring into it, by which the Pontus is sweeter and more potable than the rest of the sea. They swim like a phalanx of soldiers, eight deep and sixteen and twice as many, and they swell beneath one another, swimming each over the other to such a depth as is their breadth. Now the ways by which they are caught are countless, for it is possible to whet iron against them and to scatter drugs, and a small net has sufficed for one who is content with a small part of the shoal; but the best is this kind of hunting. Someone keeps watch from a high pole, quick at reckoning and keen of sight, for his eyes must be fixed on the sea and reach as far as possible, and if he sees the fish entering, he needs a very loud shout to those in the boats, and he tells the number and the myriads of them; and the others, fencing them off with a deep, closing net, take a splendid catch, by which the leader of the hunt is ready to grow rich. Look at the painting now, for you will see these very things being done. The watcher looks at the sea, sending his eyes out to grasp the number; and in the grey bloom of the sea the colours of the fish appear — those above seem black, those next less so, those after them already deceive the sight, then are shadowy, then watery to guess at; for the sight, as it descends into the water, is blunted in making out what is in it. And the company of fishermen are merry and tawny in colour from the heat, and one binds his oar, one rows with arm well swollen, one urges on his neighbour, one strikes the man who is not rowing, and a shout has gone up among the fishermen, for the fish have now fallen into the net, and some they have taken, some they are taking. And, at a loss what to do with the multitude, they even open part of the net and allow some to escape and slip through, so far do they luxuriate in the hunting.
PINDAR.

I suppose it is a marvel to you that the bees are painted so minutely, with proboscis plainly visible, and feet and wings and the colour of their dress, no disorder in them, the painting picking them out variously to match nature. Why, then, are the wise creatures not in their hives? And why in the city? They are revelling at the doors of Daiphantus — for Pindar has now been born, as you see — to mould him from infancy, that he may be tuneful and musical; and they do these things. For the babe is laid in laurel and sprays of myrtle, the father reckoning that the boy will prove sacred from the signs by which cymbals resounded through the house when he was born, and drums were heard from Rhea, and the Nymphs were said to have danced for him and Pan to have leapt up; and they say that, when Pindar came to composing, Pan neglected his leaping and sang the songs of Pindar. Rhea is wrought as a statue and is set up at his very doors, and the statue, I think, seems even to be of stone, the painting here being made hard and — what else? — carved. He brings the Nymphs too, dewy and such as come from springs, while Pan dances out a certain rhythm, his look bright and nothing wrathful in his nose. And the bees within busy themselves about the babe, putting honey upon him and drawing up their stings for fear of stinging him. Perhaps they come from Hymettus, and from the rich and far-famed places, for this too, I think, they instilled into Pindar.
SEMELE.

Thunder in a hard form, and Lightning shooting flame from her eyes, and raging fire from heaven that has laid hold of a tyrant's house, touch upon a story such as this, if you are not ignorant of it. A cloud of fire, encompassing Thebes, breaks upon the roof of Cadmus when Zeus came in revel to Semele; and Semele, as it seems to us, is destroyed, while Dionysus is born, I think, by Zeus, beside the fire. And the form of Semele appears dimly through, as she goes up to heaven, and the Muses there will sing her praises; but Dionysus leaps from his mother as her womb is rent, and himself makes the murky fire bright, like a star, flashing. The flame, parting asunder, sketches out for Dionysus a cave more pleasant than any in Assyria or Lydia; for tendrils have blossomed about it, and clusters of ivy, and already vines too, and trees of the thyrsus springing up from the willing earth, so that some of them are even in the fire. Nor need we wonder if Earth crowns the fire with a garland in honour of Dionysus, she who will revel with him in the Bacchic rite and will give him wine to draw from springs and milk to draw as from breasts, the one from the clod, the other from the rock. Hear Pan, how he seems to sing of Dionysus on the peaks of Cithaeron, leaping in his evoe. But Cithaeron laments, in the form of a man, the woes soon to be in him, and bears a wreath of ivy slanting from his head, for he is crowned with it much against his will; and Megaera plants a fir beside him and brings up a spring of water over the blood, I think, of Actaeon and Pentheus.
THE GYRAEAN ROCKS.

The rocks rising from the deep, and the sea boiling about them, and the hero looking terrible upon the rocks and having a certain pride against the sea — this is the Locrian Ajax, whose own ship has been struck; and, leaping from it as it caught fire, he has come to grips with the waves, breaking through some, drawing others after him, baling some off with his breast; and having met the Gyrae — the Gyrae are rocks rising up out of the Aegean gulf — he utters overweening words against the gods, boasting; whereupon Poseidon himself sets out against the Gyrae, terrible, my boy, and full of storm and with his locks lifted up. And yet once he fought as ally to the Locrian at Ilium, when he was sober and sparing of the gods, and gave him strength with his sceptre; but now, since he sees him insolent, he brings the trident against him, and the neck of the rock that holds up Ajax shall be struck, so that he may shake him off, insolence and all. This, then, is the story of the painting; but the vividness: the sea is white with waves, the rocks are sea-washed from being for ever sprayed, fire darts up from the middle of the ship, into which the wind, blowing, makes the ship still sail, as if using the fire for a sail; and Ajax, like one recovering from drunkenness, gazes round upon the deep, seeing neither ship nor land, and does not even fear Poseidon as he approaches, but seems still to be straining, for strength has not yet left his arms, and his neck stands up as against Hector and the Trojans. Poseidon, then, driving in his trident, shall break off the fragment of the rock together with Ajax, while the remaining Gyrae shall stay, as long as there is sea, and shall stand inviolate for Poseidon.
ARIADNE.

That Theseus, dealing unjustly — though some say it was not unjustly, but at the bidding of Dionysus — left Ariadne sleeping on the island of Dia, you have perhaps heard even from your nurse, for they are wise in such matters and weep over them whenever they please. I need not say, then, that Theseus is the one in the ship and Dionysus the one on the land, nor, treating you as ignorant, would I turn you to the figure on the rocks, how she lies in soft sleep; nor is it enough to praise the painter for the things by which another too might be praised, for it is easy for anyone to paint Ariadne beautiful and Theseus beautiful, and there are countless figures of Dionysus for those who wish to paint or model — even a small touch of which captures the god; for the clusters of ivy that are his wreath are a mark of Dionysus, even if the workmanship be poor, and a horn growing out from the temples reveals Dionysus, and a leopard appearing somewhere is again a symbol of the god. But this Dionysus is painted from love alone; for his flowered gear and thyrsi and fawn-skins are flung aside as out of season, and the Bacchae are not using cymbals now, nor are the Satyrs piping; rather even Pan checks his leaping, that he may not break the maiden's sleep; and clothing himself in a sea-purple robe and crowning his head with roses, Dionysus comes to Ariadne, "drunk with love," as the Teian poet says. And Theseus is indeed in love, but with the smoke of Athens, and Ariadne he no longer knows, nor ever knew; I say he has forgotten even the Labyrinth, and could not say for what he ever sailed to Crete, so wholly does he look at the things before his prow. But look at Ariadne, or rather at her sleep: her breast is bare to the navel, her neck is thrown back and her throat is soft, the right armpit is wholly visible, but the other hand rests on her cloak, lest the wind put her to any shame. What, Dionysus, and how sweet is her breathing! Whether it smells of apples or of grapes, you will tell when you have kissed her.
THESSALY.

The look of the painting plays the Egyptian, but its story is not Egyptian but, I think, Thessalian; for the Egyptians have their land from the Nile, but the Peneus of old did not allow the Thessalians to have land, mountains being thrown round the plains and the stream flooding them, since it had no outlet. Poseidon, then, will break the mountains with his trident and make gates for the river. For he stands now at this labour, contending with it and uncovering the plains, and his hand is lifted to break them through, while the mountains, before being struck, part to the measure sufficient for the river. And, as the art contends for vividness, the right side of Poseidon is at once drawn back and advanced, and threatens the blow not from the hand but from the whole body. He is painted not dark blue, nor of the sea, but a man of the mainland; and so he welcomes the plains, seeing them smooth and broad like the seas. The river too rejoices, as if boasting, and, keeping his arm bent — for it is not usual for a river to stand upright — he dedicates the Titaresius as light and more potable, and agrees with Poseidon to flow out of the plains, using the road made for him. Thessaly too rises up, the water now subsiding, crowned with olive and ear of grain, and laying hold of a foal that rises with her. For she shall have a horse too from Poseidon, when the earth shall receive the effluence of the sleeping god into a horse.
PASIPHAE.

Pasiphae is in love with the bull and begs Daedalus to contrive some means of winning the beast; and he fashions a hollow cow resembling a cow of the herd to which the bull is accustomed. And what their union was, the form of the Minotaur shows, monstrously brought to completion against nature. But it is not the union that is painted now; rather this is made the workshop of Daedalus, and statues stand round him, some in their finished shape, some in the making, already striding and on the promise of walking; for the art of sculpture before Daedalus had not yet conceived this. Daedalus himself plays the Athenian both in his look, gazing as one over-wise and full of thought, and in his very attire, for he is wrapped in a grey cloak, with the bare feet that the painter has added to him — by which most of all the Athenians are adorned. He sits at the framing of the cow and makes the Loves his fellow-workers in the contrivance, as if there were something of Aphrodite owed to it. Vivid among the Loves are those, my boy, who turn the drill, and, by Zeus, those who smooth with the adze the parts of the cow not yet finished, and those who plumb the proportion on which the workmanship advances; but those at the saw have surpassed all conception and all skill, such as belongs both to the hand and to colours. For look: a saw is set into the wood and already driven through it, and these Loves are working it back and forth, the one from the ground, the other from a raised platform, both straightening up and bending forward. Let us take this as alternating, for the one has bent forward as about to rise, the other has risen as about to bend; and the one from the ground sends his breath up to his breast, while the one above fills his belly too, pressing both hands down. But Pasiphae outside, among the cattle, gazes about at the bull, thinking to draw him to her by her beauty and her robe, which shines with something divine, beyond any rainbow; and she looks helpless, for she knows what creature she loves, and has set herself to embrace the beast, but he understands nothing of her and looks at his own cow. And the bull is painted high-spirited and the leader of the herd, fine-horned and white and firm-set and deep in the throat and thick in the neck, and looking cheerfully at the cow; while she, of the herd and unconfined, is white all over upon a black head, and disdains the bull, for she shows the frisking of a maiden, as it were, fleeing the violence of a lover.
GLAUCUS OF THE SEA.

The Argo, having sailed out through the Bosporus and the Symplegades, now cleaves the midmost surge of the Pontus, and Orpheus charms the sea with his song, and it listens, and the Pontus lies beneath the song. The freight of the ship is the Dioscuri and Heracles and the sons of Aeacus and the sons of Boreas, and all that flowered of the demigod company; and the keel fitted to the ship is an ancient tree, which Zeus at Dodona used for his oracles. The purpose of the voyage is this: a golden fleece of an ancient ram lies stored among the Colchians, the ram which is said to have ferried Helle along with Phrixus through the sky; this Jason, my boy, is set the labour of taking — for a guardian dragon is coiled about it, looking terrible and disdaining sleep — and from this the ship begins, since the cause of the voyage looks toward it. And Tiphys, my boy, is the steersman, and he is said to have been the first of men to dare the disbelieved art; and Lynceus, son of Aphareus, is set at the prow, being able to see from far off and to look deep into the depths, and to be the first to perceive sunken reefs, the first to greet land appearing. But now the eye even of Lynceus seems to me to be astounded by the apparition that meets it, by which the fifty, having checked their rowing — Heracles indeed remains unmoved by the wonder, having met with many like it, but the rest, I think, say some such word of wonder; for there appears to them Glaucus of the Sea, who is said once to have dwelt in ancient Anthedon, and to have tasted a certain sea-grass, and, a wave running over him, to have been carried off into the haunts of the fishes. He prophesies, then, something great, as is likely, for he has a surplus of the art; and as for his form, the curls of his beard are wet, and white to look upon, like fountains; heavy are the locks of his hair, and they channel down over his shoulders all the sea they have drawn in; his eyebrows are shaggy, and joined to one another like a single one. Ah, his arm, how exercised against the sea, ever falling upon the waves and smoothing them for his swimming! Ah, his breast, how down is sown over it, flourishing with sea-mosses and seaweed, while the belly lies beneath, shifting and now passing away! That Glaucus is a fish in his remaining part is shown by the tail-fins lifted up and curving toward the loins, and their crescent shape has a kind of sea-purple bloom. And halcyons fly round about him, at once singing of the men out of whom both they and Glaucus were transformed, and at once showing Orpheus their own song, through which not even the sea is without music.
HIPPODAMEIA.

This is the amazement at Oenomaus the Arcadian, and these are they who cry out over it — for you hear it, I think — and there is Arcadia and so much of the Peloponnese as belongs to it. The chariot has fallen, shattered by the craft of Myrtilus; it is drawn by four horses, for this was not yet ventured for war, but the games knew it and honoured it; and the Lydians, being most fond of horses, already had four-horse chariots and charioteers in the time of Pelops, and afterward laid hold of the four-poled car and are said to have been the first to have the team of eight. Look, boy, at the horses of Oenomaus, how terrible and violent they are at the charge, and full of frenzy and foam — and this you would find chiefly among the Arcadians — and how black they are, since they were yoked for absurd and ill-omened ends; but the horses of Pelops, how white they are and obedient to the rein, companions of persuasion and neighing something gentle and intelligent of the victory; and Oenomaus, how, like Diomedes the Thracian, he lies a barbarian and savage in form. And I think you will not disbelieve about Pelops, that Poseidon once admired him for his bloom as he poured wine for the gods on Sipylus, and, admiring him, set him up with this very chariot when he was already a youth. The chariot crosses the sea as if it were land, and not a drop leaps from it to the axle, but it lies steady beneath the horses, like the land. Now the race Pelops and Hippodameia win, both standing on the chariot and yoked together there; and they are so overcome by each other that they are on the point of embracing. And he is arrayed in the Lydian and luxurious manner, in the age and bloom you saw a little before, when he asked the horses of Poseidon; she is arrayed in the bridal manner, just now uncovering her cheek, since she has been won over to come to a husband. Alpheus too leaps up from his eddy, lifting out a wreath of wild olive for Pelops as he drives up to the bank. And the monuments in the race-course — there the suitors were buried, whom Oenomaus, slaying them, put off the marriage of his daughter, to thirteen young men already. But the earth now puts forth flowers about the monuments, that those too may have some share in seeming to be crowned at the punishment of Oenomaus.
PALAEMON.

The people sacrificing at the Isthmus, who would be those from Corinth; and this king of the people — let us suppose him Sisyphus; and this precinct of Poseidon, faintly resounding to the sea, for the foliage of the pines sings this — these signify some such thing, my boy. Ino, falling from the land, will use the one part, her own self, to be Leucothea and of the circle of the Nereids, the other, that of her child, the land will use to be Palaemon the babe. And already she puts in toward it upon a docile dolphin, and the dolphin, spreading his back beneath, carries the sleeping child, gliding noiselessly through the calm, lest he fall out of his sleep; and as he approaches, a sanctuary breaks open along the Isthmus, the land having parted asunder by Poseidon's act, who, it seems to me, foretold to this Sisyphus the inward voyage of the child and that he must sacrifice to him. And he sacrifices this black bull, having dragged it, I think, from the herd of Poseidon.
