Now the rite of the sacrifice, and the dress of those sacrificing, and the offerings to the dead, my boy, and the slaying, let these be laid up for the mysteries of Palaemon, for the matter is solemn and quite secret, as Sisyphus the wise made him a god; for the intentness of his look shows him already wise. As for the form of Poseidon, if he had been about to break the Gyraean rocks or the Thessalian mountains, he would somewhere have been painted terrible and as if striking; but, making Melicertes his guest, that he may have him in the land, he smiles as the child puts in to harbour, and bids the Isthmus open out its breast and become a home for Melicertes. And the Isthmus, my boy, is painted in the form of a spirit, reclining himself upon the land, and is ordained by nature to lie midway between the Aegean and the Adriatic, as if bridged across upon the seas. He has a youth on his right, Lechaeum, I think, and maidens on his left, Cenchreae perhaps. These are beautiful seas, and calm enough, and they sit beside the land that shows forth the Isthmus.
THE BACCHAE.

Painted here, my boy, are the things on Cithaeron too — choruses of Bacchae, and rocks streaming wine, and nectar from the grape-clusters, and how the earth makes the clod rich with milk; and see, ivy creeps, and serpents stand erect, and thyrsi, and trees, I think, dripping honey. And here is the fir, fallen to the ground, the work of women under Dionysus, a great thing — fallen, having shaken off Pentheus to the Bacchae in the form of a lion; and they tear the quarry, his mother there and his mother's sisters, some rending off his arms, one dragging her son by the hair. You would say that they are even shrieking, so full of evoe is their breathing. Dionysus himself stands in a place overlooking all this, having filled his cheek with anger, and has driven the women on to madness with frenzy; and so they do not even see what is being done, and however much Pentheus supplicates, they say they hear a lion roaring. These are the things on the mountain; but those near at hand are these — Thebes already, and the roof of Cadmus, and a dirge over the prey; and the kindred fit the corpse together, in case it might somehow be saved for the tomb. There lies the head of Pentheus too, no longer doubtful but such as for Dionysus himself to pity, very young and soft of cheek and ruddy of hair — hair which no ivy roofed, nor any tendril of bryony or vine, nor did any pipe set it tossing, nor frenzy. By these things he had been made strong, and he made them strong; but his madness was precisely this, not to be mad along with Dionysus. Pitiable too let us hold the case of the women, for what things they did not know on Cithaeron, what things here they recognize. Not only their madness has left them, but also the strength by which they raged. For on Cithaeron you see how, full of the contest, they are borne along, raising the echo of the mountain; but here they grow calm and come to a sense of their Bacchic deeds, sinking to the earth, the head of one weighing down upon her knees, of another upon her shoulder; and Agave has set herself to embrace her son, but shrinks from touching him. There clings to her the boy's blood, some on her hands, some on her cheek, some on the bare part of her breast. And Harmonia and Cadmus are there, but not such as they were, for they are already becoming serpents from the thighs, and scales already cover them; their feet are gone, their haunches gone, and the change of form creeps upward. And they are struck with horror and embrace each other, as if holding fast the remaining parts of their bodies, that those at least might not slip from them.
THE ISLANDS.

Will you, my boy, that we converse about these islands as if from a ship, sailing round them in spring, when Zephyr makes the sea cheerful, breathing of his own breeze? But see that you willingly forget the land, and this will seem to you a sea neither lifted up and tossing its mane, nor flat and calm, but navigable and as it were breathing. See, we have embarked — for you consent, I suppose.

The sea, as you see, is wide, and there are islands in it, by Zeus, not Lesbos, nor Imbros or Lemnos, but herding and small, like villages or stations or, by Zeus, farmsteads of the sea. The first of them is strong and steep and walled by nature, lifting up a peak to all-seeing Poseidon, full of streams and moist, and feeding bees with mountain flowers, which the Nereids too are likely to gather when they play upon the sea. The next island, which is flat and earthy, fishermen inhabit together with farmers, and they hold a market with each other, some of their crops, some of what they have caught; and they have set up this Poseidon as a farmer, on plough and yoke, to reckon for him the produce of the earth; and, that Poseidon might not appear too much a man of the mainland, a ship's prow is set upon the plough, and he breaks the earth as if sailing. The two islands next to these were once both one, but, broken by the sea, were carried apart by the breadth of a river between them; and this you can know even from the painting, my boy, for you see the sundered parts of the island similar and proportioned to each other, and as it were hollows fitting projections. This too Europe once suffered about Thessalian Tempe; for earthquakes, breaking open there too the harmony of the mountains, left their mark upon the severed parts, and the lairs of the rocks are still plainly similar to the rocks fitted out of them, and the wood, such as was likely to follow when the mountains split, is not yet undiscoverable, for there still remain the beds of the trees. Such, then, let us suppose to be the experience of the island; and a bridge is thrown across the strait, so that it appears one by it, and part of the bridge is sailed under, part driven over with wagons; for you see, I suppose, those passing across it, that they are both travellers and sailors. But the island near at hand, my boy, let us hold a marvel, for fire smoulders all beneath it, having crept into the caverns and recesses of the island, through which, as through pipes, the flame breaks out and makes terrible torrents, from which fall rivers of fire, great and surging upon the sea. And to one who wishes to philosophize about such things, the island, providing a mixture of asphalt and sulphur, when it is eaten away by the brine, is set ablaze by many winds, drawing up from the sea the things that excite the fuel; but the painting, praising the poets, inscribes a myth upon the island too — that a giant was once cast down there, and, as he was struggling against death, the island was set upon him for a bond, but that he has not yet yielded, but fights on from beneath the earth, and breathes out this fire with a threat. This, they say, Typho too desires in Sicily, and Enceladus in this part of Italy, whom continents and islands press down, not yet dead but ever dying. And you may, my boy, suppose that you have not been left out of the battle, by looking up at the summit of the mountain; for the things appearing on it are Zeus hurling thunderbolts at the giant, who already gives up, yet still trusts the earth, while the earth too is worn out, since Poseidon will not let her stand. He has thrown a mist about them, that they may appear as having become so rather than as becoming. As for the hill round which we sail, a dragon dwells on it, the guardian, I think, of some treasure that lies beneath the earth. For this beast is said to be friendly to gold, and whatever it sees that is golden it loves and cherishes; the fleece in Colchis and the apples of the Hesperides, since they appeared golden, two sleepless dragons kept and made their own; and the dragon of Athena, who still even now dwells on the Acropolis, seems to me to have welcomed the Athenian people for the gold which they made into grasshoppers for their hair. And here the dragon himself is golden, for he thrusts his head out over the lair, in fear, I think, for the wealth below. And this island, roofed over with ivy and bryony and vines, says it is dedicated to Dionysus, but that Dionysus is away now and revelling somewhere on the mainland, having entrusted to Silenus the secret things here. The secret things are these cymbals lying face-up, and golden mixing-bowls overturned, and pipes still warm, and the drums lying soundless; and Zephyr as it were lifts the fawn-skins from the earth, and of the serpents some are twined among the thyrsi, others, relaxed by the wine, sleep and let the Bacchae gird themselves with them. As for the clusters, some swell with juice, some darken, some are unripe, some seem mere blossom, Dionysus having contrived the seasons of the vines so that he may always be harvesting. And the clusters are so abundant that they even hang from the rocks and droop over the sea, and birds of the sea and of the mainland fly up to gather the fruit; for Dionysus offers the vine common to all save the owl, which alone among the eaters of clusters he rejects, since it slanders wine to men; for if an infant child, still wineless, should eat the eggs of the owl, it hates wine all its life, and would not drink, and fears the drunken. But you, my boy, are so bold as not even to fear this Silenus, the guardian of the island, drunk and laying hold of the Bacchant. But she does not deign to look at him; rather, in love with Dionysus, she fashions him in her mind and figures him forth and sees him though he is not present; for the character of the eyes in the Bacchant is aloft, yet not outside erotic thoughts. These mountains nature has joined together and made an island, shaggy and full of wood, of tall cypress and pine and fir and oak and cedar; for the trees too are painted each in its own manner. The game-haunted parts of the island boar-hunters track out, and deer-shooters, lifting their lances against the beasts, and some with bows; and they carry knives too, my boy, and clubs, those who fight at close quarters and are bold; and these nets are stretched through the wood, some to enfold a beast, some to bind it, some to check its run; and some of the beasts are taken, some fight, some have caught the one who threw, and every young man's arm is busy, and the dogs raise a cry along with the men, so that even the echo, they say, joins the hunting's revel. The great trees the woodcutters cut up with broad strokes, and one lifts the axe, one has driven it in, one whets it, having taken it blunted by striking, one examines the fir for a mast, judging the tree by reference to the ship, one cuts the young and straight trees for oars. The sheer rock, and the tribe of sea-gulls, and the bird in their midst are painted from such a reason as this. Men attack the sea-gulls, by Zeus, not for the sake of the flesh, for black and unwholesome and not pleasant even to the hungry is the flesh of them, but they provide for the sons of physicians a stomach such as to make those who taste of it good eaters and light, since they are sleepy and easily inflamed, for at night a light flashes within them. So they win over the cormorant-bird, on a share of the catch, to be a steward and to keep watch before them. The cormorant is a sea-bird, but a good bird and free of trouble, and feeble at catching anything, but strong for sleep, and sleeps little; and so it hires out its eyes to those gulls. Whenever, then, they fly off to their feast, the cormorant keeps house about the rock, and they come back at evening, bringing him a tithe of what they have caught, and they sleep now around him who does not sleep, nor would ever be overcome by sleep, unless they themselves wish it. And if it perceives some treachery approaching, the cormorant cries out clear and shrill, and they, lifted up at the signal, flee, holding up their steward, in case he should fail in flight. But here he stands and watches over the gulls. And the part of him that stands in the midst of the birds is the Proteus among the seals, while his not sleeping is beyond Proteus. And here, my boy, we too have come to harbour; and what the name of the island is I do not know, but it should, for my part, be named the Golden Isle, unless the poets have devised such a title in vain for all things beautiful and marvellous. It is inhabited, so far as a small palace can be received, for no one will plough here, nor tend vines, but it abounds in springs, of which some it gives forth pure and cold, some, after heating them, so abundant that they even flood upon the sea; for this surge is heaved up by the springs, boiling and as it were leaping and springing up as from a cauldron, around which this island is set. As to the marvel of the issuing of the springs, whether one should think it belongs to the land or assign it to the sea, this Proteus will decide, for he has come to give judgment on it; but let us look at the inhabited parts of the island; for there is settled in it the image of a beautiful and splendid city, as much as a single house, and a royal child is reared within, and the city is his plaything. For there are theatres, as many as can hold him and these his playmates; and a hippodrome is built, sufficient for the Maltese puppies to run round, for he makes these his horses and harnesses them to yoke and chariot, to be driven by these monkeys, whom the child counts his servants; and this hare, lodged here yesterday, I think, is held by a scarlet leash, like a dog, but does not deign to be bound and wishes to slip its bonds, trusting in its forefeet; and a parrot and a jay, in a wickerwork cage, sing in the island like Sirens, and the one sings what it knows, the other what it learns.
THE TYRRHENIANS.

A sacred ship and a pirate ship. The one Dionysus steers; the other Tyrrhenian pirates of the surrounding sea have boarded. The sacred ship is in Bacchic frenzy, for Dionysus revels in it and the Bacchae raise their cry, and harmony, such as belongs to the rites, sounds across the sea, and the sea offers her own back to Dionysus, like the land of the Lydians; but in the other ship they are raving and forget their rowing, and the hands of many of them are already lost. What is the painting? The Tyrrhenians, my boy, lie in wait for Dionysus, a report having come to them that he was womanish, and a wandering beggar, and his ship golden with the wealth in it; that Lydian women attended him, and Satyrs and pipers, and an old man carrying the fennel-rod, and Maronean wine and Maron himself; and hearing that Pans sailed with him in the form of goats, they thought to carry off the Bacchae and to leave to those Pans the goats that the land of the Tyrrhenians pastures. Now the pirate ship sails in warlike fashion, for it is fitted with cat-heads and a ram, and there are iron grappling-hands upon it, and spear-points and sickles upon poles; and that it may strike terror into those it meets and may appear to them some monster, it is painted with grey-green colours, and it looks, as it were, with grim eyes upon the prow, while the stern is slender and crescent-shaped, like the tails of fishes. But the ship of Dionysus seems in other respects likened to a rock, and is seen scaled toward the stern, with cymbals fitted alternately upon it, so that, even if the Satyrs should ever sleep from the wine, Dionysus might not sail without sound; and the prow is likened to a golden leopard and is wrought into its shape. Dionysus has a friendship with this animal, since it is the hottest of animals and leaps lightly, like a votary of the rite. You see, indeed, the very beast sailing with Dionysus and leaping at the Tyrrhenians though he has not yet given the command. And here a thyrsus has sprung up from the middle of the ship, doing the work of the mast, and sails have been raised, sea-purple, glistening in the breeze, and golden Bacchae are woven into them, with the scenes of Dionysus in Tmolus and in Lydia. That the ship should appear roofed over with vine and ivy, and clusters hanging above it, is a marvel, but more marvellous is the spring of wine, as though the hollow ship gave it forth. . . . They run upon the Tyrrhenians, shapes of dolphins not yet tame, nor native to that sea; and one has dark-blue sides, another slippery breast, in another a crest grows along the back, another sends out tail-fins, and one has the head already gone, another still has it, in one the hand is webbed, and one cries out over his feet as they depart. But Dionysus, from the prow, laughs at all this and bids the Tyrrhenians take from men the forms of fishes, but from base men the characters of good ones. At any rate, a little later Palaemon will ride upon a dolphin, and he not even awake, but lying on his back asleep upon it; and Arion at Taenarum proves that dolphins are companions to men, and friends of song, and such as to array themselves against pirates on behalf of men and of music.
THE CYCLOPS.

Those reaping the corn and harvesting the vines neither ploughed, my boy, nor planted these things, but the earth sends them up to them of itself; for they are Cyclopes, for whom, I know not why, the poets will have the earth to bear of its own accord what it bears; and they are made shepherds too, the earth pasturing their flocks, whose milk they reckon both drink and meat. They know neither market nor council-house, nor house, but inhabit the clefts of the mountain. Now let the rest be; but Polyphemus, son of Poseidon, the most savage of them, dwells here, stretching a single eyebrow over his one eye, and treading upon his lip with his broad nose, and feeding on men, like the savage among lions. But now he abstains from such food, that he may not appear gluttonous and unpleasing, for he is in love with Galatea as she plays upon this sea, watching her from the mountain; and his pipe is still under his arm and at rest, but he has a shepherd's song, how she is white and skittish and sweeter than the unripe grape, and how he rears fawns and bear-cubs for Galatea. He sings these things beneath an oak, not knowing where his flocks pasture, nor how many they are, nor where the land is. And he is painted still mountainous and terrible, shaking his hair erect and abundant like a pine, and showing jagged teeth from his ravening jaw, and shaggy in breast and belly and down to the nails on his feet; and he says he looks gentle, since he is in love, but he looks savage and still crouching, like beasts overcome by necessity. But she plays on the soft sea, yoking a team of four dolphins that work together and breathe in unison, and maiden handmaids of Triton, attendants of Galatea, drive them, curbing them if they do anything wanton and contrary to the rein. And over her head she lifts a sea-purple scarf against the Zephyr, to be a shade for herself and a sail for the chariot, from which a certain gleam comes upon her forehead and her head, yet not sweeter than the bloom of her cheek. Her hair is not loosed to the Zephyr, for it is wet and too strong for the wind. And lo, her right elbow stands out, bending the white forearm and resting the fingers on her soft shoulder, and her arms swell gently, and her breast rises up, nor does beauty desert even the part above the knee. The foot, my boy, and the grace that ends with it upon the sea, is painted, and grazes the sea as if steering the chariot. A marvel are her eyes, for they look at something beyond the horizon, passing away with the length of the deep.
THE SATYRS.

The place is dark, so far as the springs and the cave; and Marsyas is out of the way, either pasturing his flocks or after the contest. Do not praise the water; for though it is painted potable and calm, you will meet with a more potable one in Olympus. He sleeps after the piping, delicate among delicate flowers, mingling his sweat with the dew of the meadow; and Zephyr calls him forth, breathing upon his hair, while he breathes back against the wind, drawing the breath up from his breast. And piping reeds lie now beside Olympus, and the little iron tools too with which the pipes are bored. A herd of Satyrs, in love with him, gaze upon the youth, flushed and grinning, one begging to touch his breast, one to cling to his neck, one longing to snatch a kiss; and they scatter flowers upon him and worship him as a statue; and the cleverest of them, drawing out the tongue of one of the still-warm pipes, eats it, and so thinks he kisses Olympus, and says he has also tasted his breath.
PHORBAS.

The river, my boy, is the Cephisus of Boeotia, and not of the unmusical kind; and beside it the Phlegyans, barbarians, are encamped, not yet a city. As for those boxing — you see, I think, Apollo, while the other is Phorbas, whom the Phlegyans set up as king, since he was great beyond all and the most savage of the nation. Apollo boxes against him for the passes; for, having seized the road straight to Phocis and Delphi, no one any longer sacrifices at Pytho, nor brings paeans to the god, and oracles and prophecies and the utterances of the tripod have all failed. He plays the brigand, having cut himself off from the other Phlegyans; for this oak, my boy, he has made his house, and the Phlegyans come to him to be judged, no doubt, in this his palace. And those going to the temple he seizes — the old and the children he sends to the common stock of the Phlegyans to be plundered and ransomed, but with the stronger he strips for the contest, and some he throws in wrestling, some he outruns, some he takes in the pancratium and by his great casts of the discus; and, cutting off their heads, he hangs them on the oak and lives beneath this gore, and they hang from the boughs, rotting; and some you see dry, some fresh, and some have shrunk to skulls, and they grin and seem to wail as the wind blows into them. While he is high-minded over these Olympic contests of his, Apollo comes, having likened himself to a boxer-youth; and as for the form of the god, he is painted unshorn, my boy, with his locks bound up, that he may box with head well-girt, and rays rise up from his forehead, and his cheek sends forth a smile blended with anger, and the glances of his eyes are well-aimed and lift themselves up along with his hands; and his hands are bound with the thongs, sweeter than if there were crowns about them. He has already boxed him, for the right hand, planted in its blow, still shows the hand active and not yet relaxing the figure by which it conquered; and Phorbas lies, and how much of the ground he covers a poet will tell, and the wound has gone to his temple, and the blood is given forth as from a spring. And he is painted savage and swinish in form, such as to feast on strangers rather than to kill them. And the fire from heaven, a thunderbolt, is borne upon the oak to burn the tree together, yet not to take away the memory upon it; for the place in which these things are, my boy, is still "the Oak-Heads."
OLYMPUS.

For whom do you pipe, Olympus? And what work has music in a solitude? No shepherd is by you, no goatherd, nor do you pipe for the nymphs, who would dance prettily to the pipe; but having learned I know not what delight, you take pleasure in the water on the rock and look into it. What share have you in it? For it neither murmurs to your pipe nor measures out the day for us — we who should wish you to draw out your piping even into the night. And if you are examining your beauty, never mind the water, for we are more competent to tell all that is in you. Your eye is bright, and many are its incitements to the pipe; an eyebrow is set about it, marking the meaning of the strains; the cheek seems to throb and, as it were, to dance to the melody; the breath lifts nothing of the face, since it is engaged in the pipe; and your hair is neither idle nor lies, as on a city youth, sleek with oil, but is roused by the dryness, yet shows nothing parched, amid the sharp and green pine. For the wreath is beautiful and able to lend grace to those in their prime, but let flowers spring for maidens and work their blush upon women. I say that your breast too is full not of breath only but of musical thought and consideration of the strains. Thus far the water paints you, stooping into it from the rock; but had it painted you standing, it would not have shown the parts beneath the breast comely, for the reflections in water are shallow, since lengths shrink together in them. And that your reflection too should be washed about, let it be both from the pipe blowing down upon the spring, and from Zephyr — all these things — through whom you also are in the piping, and the pipe in the breathing, and the spring in being piped to.
ATLAS.

Even with Atlas Heracles contended, without Eurystheus' command, thinking that he would carry the sky better than Atlas; for he saw him bowed and pressed down and sunk upon one knee, with little left him of standing, while he himself could even lift up the sky and set it firm, taking it upon himself for a long time. This ambition, however, he nowhere shows, but says that he grieves with Atlas for what he toils at, and that he would share the burden with him. And Atlas has so gladly laid hold of Heracles as to supplicate him to endure these things. And the one is painted exhausted, so that one may infer from the sweat how much drips from him, and may understand that his arm is trembling, while the other is in love with the labour. This is shown both by the eagerness of his face and by the club thrown down and the hands demanding the labour. As for the shadows, those of Heracles are not yet worth marvelling at, if they are strong — for the figures of those lying down, and the upright ones too, are easily shadowed, and to be exact about these is not yet wise — but the shadows of Atlas approach wisdom, for, as he is thus crouched together, they fall together with one another and do not at all darken the projecting parts, but make light about the hollows and the recesses. The belly, too, of Atlas, even as he stoops forward, one can see, and can understand it as panting, and the things in the heaven that he carries are painted in such an aether as stands about them, and one can make out the bull — the bull that is in the heaven — and the bears, such as are seen there, and the winds. For some are painted with one another, some out of one another, and some have friendship toward one another, while some seem to preserve the strife that is in heaven. Now, then, you will lay these down, Heracles, but not long after you will live with them in heaven, drinking and embracing the form of Hebe; for you shall wed the youngest and oldest of the gods, since through her even those gods are young.
MIDAS.

The Satyr sleeps; let us speak about him with lowered voice, lest he wake and break up the scene. Midas has hunted him with wine in Phrygia, about these very mountains, as you see, having mixed wine into the spring in which he lies, slavering out the wine in his sleep. Now of Satyrs the violence is delightful when they dance, and delightful the buffoonery when they smile, and the noble ones are amorous and win over the Lydian women, coaxing them with craft. And this too is theirs: they are painted hard and full-blooded, with excessive ears and hollow at the haunch, high-spirited in everything and horses as to their tails. The Satyr that is the prey of Midas is painted with all these features, but sleeps under the wine, drawing his breath as in drunkenness; and the spring has been drunk by him more easily than another a cup, while the Nymphs dance, mocking the Satyr for sleeping. How dainty is Midas, how indolent — he cares for his headband and his curl and carries a thyrsus and wears a gold-bordered robe! And see, large ears too, by which his eyes, seeming pleasant, appear drowsy and draw the pleasure off into sluggishness — the painting hinting earnestly that these things have already been let slip and spread abroad among men in the reed, since the earth did not keep what it heard.
ANTAEUS.

Such dust as there is in wrestling, that, by a spring of oil, and of two athletes one binding his ear, the other loosing the lion-skin from his shoulder, and convenient hills and pillars and hollow letters — this is Libya and Antaeus, whom the earth sent up to harm strangers, by a brigand's wrestling, I think. While he is busy with this and burying those he destroyed about this very wrestling-ground, as you see, the painting brings Heracles, having now taken these golden apples and being sung of for those of the Hesperides — for it was no marvel of Heracles to take them, but the dragon — and, without so much as bending his knee, they say, he strips for Antaeus in the panting of his journey, straining his eyes to some thought and as it were a consideration of the wrestling, and he has put a rein on his spirit not to carry him outside of reason. But Antaeus, disdainful, is lifted up, "children of wretches," or some such thing, he seems to say to Heracles, strengthening himself with insolence. And if Heracles had cared for wrestling too, he was made by nature no otherwise than as he is painted; and he is painted strong, such a one too as is full of art by reason of the good harmony of his body, and he would be both huge and beyond human in form. There is in him too a bloom of blood, and the veins are as in the throes of some spirit that still lies sunk within them. But Antaeus, my boy, you fear, I think, for he resembles some beast, falling little short of being equal in length and breadth, and the neck is set upon the shoulders, the most of which comes to the neck; and the arm is fashioned as the shoulders are; the breast and belly are these hammered things, and the unstraightness of the shin, but its ignoble strength, knows Antaeus to be strong indeed, yet compact and outside of art. Moreover Antaeus is black, the sun having gone to his dyeing. These, then, are the things of both for the wrestling. But you see them wrestling too, or rather having wrestled, and Heracles in the act of mastering. He throws him above the earth, because the earth wrestled along with Antaeus, arching herself and heaving him up whenever he lay down. So Heracles, at a loss what to do with the earth, has caught Antaeus about the middle, above the flank, where the ribs are, and, setting him upright upon his thigh, and joining his hands, has put his forearm beneath the slack and panting belly and squeezes out the breath and slays Antaeus with the sharp ribs turned toward the liver. And you see, I suppose, the one wailing and looking to the earth that no longer avails him, and Heracles strong and smiling at the deed. The summit of the mountain do not look at idly, but suppose that there, upon it, gods have a watch-place over the contest; for a golden cloud too is painted, beneath which, I think, they are encamped, and this Hermes comes to Heracles to crown him, because he plays the wrestling well for him.
NARCISSUS.

The spring paints Narcissus, and the painting the spring and all that belongs to Narcissus. A youth just returned from the hunt stands over a spring, drawing out of himself a kind of longing and in love with his own beauty; and he flashes, as you see, into the water. Now the cave is of Achelous and the Nymphs, and it is painted as is fitting, for the statues are of a rude art and of the local stone, and some are worn away by time, while others children of cowherds or shepherds have chipped, being still infants and insensible of the god. Nor is the spring unvisited by Dionysus, since he has revealed it, as it were, to the women of the wine-press; at any rate, it is roofed over with vine and ivy and beautiful tendrils, and shares in clusters of grapes, whence the thyrsi come, and clever birds revel over it, each according to its own harmony, and white flowers grow beside the spring, not yet in being but springing up over the youth. The painting, honouring the truth, sheds even a kind of dew from the flowers, on which a bee too has settled — I do not know whether deceived by the painting, or whether we ought to be deceived into thinking it real. But let that be. As for you, however, youth, no painting deceived you, nor are you glued fast to colours or wax; you do not know that the water has moulded you just as you saw it, nor do you detect the spring's trick, though you need only nod and shift your shape, and move your hand a little, and not stand in the same place — but you, as if you had met a comrade, wait for what is to come from there. Will the spring, then, hold converse with you in a fable? But this youth hears nothing of us, and has fallen upon the water with ears and eyes alike; we ourselves, however, as the figure is painted, let us speak. The youth stands upright at rest, with his feet crossed, and supports himself with the spear fixed in his left hand, while his right hand is drawn back to his hip both to hold him up and to make a figure, the buttocks jutting out by reason of the leftward inclination of the body. The hand shows air at the part where the elbow is bent, a wrinkle at the part where the wrist is twisted, and casts a shadow that gathers into the palm; and the rays of the shadow are slanting because of the inward turn of the fingers. The breathing in the breast I cannot tell whether it is still that of the hunt, or already that of love; the eye, however, is sufficiently that of a lover, for its brightness and fierceness by nature are softened by a longing that settles upon it; and he seems perhaps to be loved in return, since the reflection looks at him as he is looked at by it. Much might be said about the hair too, had we met him at the hunt, for its movements in the running are countless, and more so when it has caught the breath of some wind; but it might find mention even now: for, since it is abundant and as it were golden, part of it the neck-tendons draw down, part is distinguished beneath the ears, part tosses upon the forehead, part flows down to the chin. And both Narcissi are alike in form, showing the same look as each other, save that the one stands out of the air, while the other has sunk beneath the spring. For the youth stands over a still water, or rather over one gazing fixedly at him and, as it were, thirsting for his beauty.
HERACLES AMONG THE PYGMIES.

As Heracles sleeps in Libya after Antaeus, the Pygmies set upon him, claiming to avenge Antaeus, for they are brothers, forsooth, of Antaeus — a brave sort, not athletes, nor equal to the contest, but earth-born and otherwise strong; and as they come up out of the earth the sand swells gently. For the Pygmies inhabit the earth like ants, and store up a market, and feed not on what is another's but on their own and self-grown, for they sow and reap and stand over a Pygmy team, and they are said to use an axe upon the corn-ear, thinking it to be trees. But, ah, their boldness — against Heracles these go, and they say they will kill him sleeping, though they would fear him not even awake. He sleeps on the soft sand, weariness having stolen over him in the wrestling, and with his whole breast he draws his breath, filling himself greedily with sleep, and Sleep himself stands over him in bodily form, making much, I think, of his own share in the fall of Heracles. Antaeus too lies there, but the art paints Heracles breathing and warm, and Antaeus dead and dry, and leaves him to the earth. The army, the Pygmies, having encompassed Heracles — this one phalanx assails the left hand, while these two companies march against the right as the stronger, and bowmen and a crowd of slingers besiege the two feet, astounded at the shin, how great it is; and those who fight against the head are stationed here — the king, since this seems to them the strongest part — and they bring up against it, as against a citadel, their engines: fire upon the hair, a mattock upon the eyes, certain doors upon the mouth and, I think, the gates of the nose, that Heracles may not breathe when the head is taken. These things are about the sleeper; but see, too, how he rises up and laughs at the danger, and, gathering all the foe together, puts them into the lion-skin and carries them, I think, to Eurystheus.
HYACINTHUS.

Read the hyacinth, for it is written there, and it says that it sprang up from the earth in honour of a beautiful youth, and it laments him along with the spring, having received its birth, I think, from him when he died; and let not the meadow put you off this, for it has grown here too, just as it sprang from the earth there. The painting says also that the youth's hair was hyacinthine, and that his blood, living in the earth and being drunk by it, dyed the flower its own colour. It flows from the head itself, where the discus has fallen upon it. Dreadful is the mischance, and not even credible to be told against Apollo; but since we have not come as sophists of the myths, nor are ready to disbelieve, but are only spectators of what is painted, let us examine the painting, and first the starting-line of the discus. A small mound has been heaped up, enough for one to stand on, which, raising the hinder and right leg, sets the foreparts inclining forward, and lightens one of the two legs, which must spring up together and move forward with the right hand. As for the figure of one casting the discus, he must turn his head to the right and bend so far as to look askance at his sides, and hurl it, as it were drawing it up and putting his whole right side into the throw. And Apollo cast the discus somewhat thus, for he could not otherwise have let it fly; but the discus, falling upon the youth, he lies beneath the very discus — a Laconian youth, straight of shin and not unpractised in running, the arm already lifting and the bloom of the bones just showing through — while Apollo, still standing at the starting-line, has turned away and looks at the ground. You will say he is rooted there, so much amazement has fallen on him. Ill-bred indeed is Zephyr, who, being indignant with him, sent the discus against the youth; and the wind thinks all this a joke and jeers from his watch-tower. You see him, I think, with winged temples and dainty form, and he carries a wreath of all flowers, and a little later he will twine the hyacinth among them.
HERACLES MAD.

Fight, my brave ones, against Heracles, and go forward! But let him spare the remaining child, two already lying dead and his hand taking aim — how beautiful for Heracles! Great is your contest, and in no way less than what he himself accomplished before his madness. But fear nothing: he is away from you, gazing at Argos and thinking that he slays the sons of Eurystheus; and I heard him in Euripides, leading chariots and bringing the goad to the horses and threatening to sack the house of Eurystheus — for madness is a deceitful thing and dreadful at leading one from things present to things not present. For these, then, this is enough; but for you it is time to attend to the painting. The chamber, on which he has rushed, holds Megara and a child still living; and baskets and lustral water and barley-grains and split wood and a mixing-bowl, the things of the household altar, are all kicked over; and the bull stands ready, and the victims of the breeds are flung beside the altar and the lion-skin. And one child has been struck in the throat, and the arrow has run out through the soft windpipe; another has been pierced to the very breast, and the barbs of the shaft have broken through the middle of the vertebrae, so that it is clear it was thrown into the side. Their cheeks are wet — and do not wonder if they shed a tear or two, for children's tears are golden, perhaps both small and great. As Heracles rages, all the household of his servants stands round, like cowherds about a maddened bull — one plotting to bind, one making a contest of holding him fast, another shouting, one hangs from his hands, one trips his heel, others leap upon him; but he has no perception of them, and he flings off those who come near and tramples them, spitting out much foam, and smiling grim and strange and fixing his eyes upon what he is doing, but carrying the intent of his gaze to the things he has been deceived into. His throat roars, and his neck fills, and the veins about it swell, through which all the supply of the disease flows up to the vital parts of the head. The Fury, who had power to do these things, you have often seen upon the stage, but here you could not see her, for she has lodged within Heracles himself, and dances through the midst of his breast, leaping within him and clouding his reason. Thus far the painting; but the poets carry the drunken revel further and bind Heracles, and that too though they say that Prometheus was loosed by him.
THE ANDRIANS.

The stream of wine in the island of Andros, and the Andrians drunk from the river, are the theme of the painting. For to the Andrians, by the gift of Dionysus, the land bursts open wine-laden and gives forth a river to them — small, if you should think of it as water, but, if as wine, a great and divine river. For one who has drawn from it may well despise the Nile and the Ister, and may even say of them that they too would seem better if, though few, they flowed of such a kind. And they sing these things, I think, women and children together, garlanded with ivy and bryony; and some dance on either bank, others lie at their ease. And it is likely that these too are part of the song: that Achelous bears reeds, and Tempe the Peneus, and Pactolus flowers besides, but that this river makes men wealthy and powerful in the marketplace and careful of their friends, and beautiful and four cubits tall out of small — for one who is sated with it may gather these gifts together and bring them into his fancy. They sing too, no doubt, that this alone of rivers is passable neither to herds nor to horses, but is poured out as wine by Dionysus, and is drunk pure, flowing for men alone. These things imagine yourself to hear, with some even singing them, their voices stammering with the wine. As for what is seen in the painting: the river lies on a couch of grape-clusters, pouring forth his stream, unmixed and swelling in his look, and thyrsi grow beside him, as reeds beside waters; and to one who passes over the land and these revels upon it, Tritons already, meeting them about the mouths, draw up the wine in shells, and some of it they drink, some they blow forth, and there are Tritons too who are drunk and dance. Dionysus also sails to the revel of Andros, and his ship is already moored, and he brings Satyrs mingled with women of the wine-press, and Silenus; and he leads Laughter and Comus, two most cheerful and convivial spirits, that the river may be most pleasantly gathered for him.
THIODAMAS.

This man is rough, and, by Zeus, in a rough land, for this is the island of Rhodes, whose roughest part is the Lindians' — a land good to give raisins and figs, but not happy for ploughing and impossible for wagons. The harsh fellow, a farmer in raw old age, conceive to be Thiodamas the Lindian, if you have anywhere heard of him. But, ah, his boldness — Thiodamas is angry with Heracles, because, coming upon him as he ploughed, he slaughtered one of the two oxen and feasts, being thoroughly accustomed to such food. For you have somewhere met Heracles in Pindar, when, coming to the house of Coronus, he eats a whole ox, so as not to count even the bones superfluous. And, coming upon Thiodamas about the time of unyoking, and bringing fire — for stones too are good to kindle — he roasts the ox, trying the flesh whether it is now soft, and all but rebukes the fire as slow. The painting is such as not to have overlooked even the look of the land, for, where the earth has given over a little of itself to be ploughed, it seems, if I understand it, not even to be poor. Heracles keeps the strong part of his mind on the ox, but gives the idle part to the curses of Thiodamas, just enough to let his cheek relax; and the farmer attacks Heracles with stones. And the fashion of his dress is Dorian, and there is dryness about his hair and grime about his forehead, and a knee and an arm such as his dearest land brings her athletes to. This is the deed of Heracles, and this Thiodamas is venerated among the Lindians; whence a plough-ox is sacrificed to Heracles, and they begin the rite with curses, such as, I think, the farmer then used; and Heracles rejoices and grants good things to the Lindians as they curse.
THE BIRTH OF HERMES.

The infant still in swaddling-clothes, who drives the cattle into the cleft of the earth — and that other who steals the arrows of Apollo — this is Hermes. Most delightful are the god's thefts; for they say that Hermes, when he was born to Maia, fell in love with stealing and knew how to do it, the god doing this in no way out of poverty, but giving rein to merriment and playing. If you wish to view him step by step, look at the things in the painting. He is born on the peaks of Olympus, at the very topmost seat of the gods; and there Homer says that one feels neither rains nor hears winds, nor is the place ever struck by snow because of its height, but that it is simply divine and free of all the sufferings of which the mountains of men partake. There the Hours tend Hermes at his birth. He has painted them too, as each is in her season, and they wrap him in swaddling-clothes, scattering the most beautiful of flowers, that his swaddling-clothes may not lack distinction; and some of them turn to the mother of Hermes lying in childbed, while he, slipping out of his swaddling-clothes, already walks and comes down from Olympus. And the mountain rejoices for him, for its smile is like that of a man. Conceive, then, that Olympus is glad because Hermes was born there. What, then, is the theft? Cattle grazing at the foot of Olympus — those, of course, with golden horns and whiter than snow, for they are dedicated to Apollo — he drives, twisting them, into a chasm of the earth, not that they should perish, but that they should be made to vanish for a single day, until it should sting Apollo; and, as if no part of what had happened were his, he slips back into his swaddling-clothes. Apollo too has come to Maia, demanding back the cattle; but she disbelieves and thinks the god is talking nonsense. Do you wish to learn what he says? For it seems to me that he shows on his face not voice only but something of speech as well, as one about to say this to Maia: "Your son wrongs me — the son you bore yesterday — for the cattle in which I delighted he has cast into the earth, I know not where in the earth; and he shall perish and be cast lower down, below the cattle." But she wonders and does not accept the speech. While they are still disputing with each other, Hermes stands behind Apollo and, leaping lightly upon his back, noiselessly undoes the bow and quiver, and in stealing escaped notice — yet was not unknown to have stolen. Here is the wisdom of the painter: for he melts Apollo and makes him rejoice. And the laughter is measured, such as settles upon the face when pleasure overcomes anger.
THE BURIAL OF ABDERUS.

Let us not, my boy, count the mares of Diomedes the labour of Heracles, since he has already taken them and crushed them with his club, and one of them lies, one gasps, one you will say is rearing up, one is falling — barbarous in their manes and shaggy to the hoof and otherwise beasts; and the mangers are full of human limbs and bones, which Diomedes used for this horse-rearing; and the horse-rearer himself is more savage to look upon than the mares beside which he has fallen. But this labour we must think the harder, both because Love, beyond the many things, imposed it on Heracles, and because there was no small toil over it; for Heracles carries Abderus half-eaten, having torn him from the mares; and they feasted on him while he was still soft and younger than Iphitus, and this one may infer from the remains too, for they still lie beautiful in the lion-skin. The tears over them, and if he embraced any of them or said anything in lament, and the heaviness of his face in mourning — let these be granted to another lover too; let a pillar also have some honour, standing over the tomb of a beautiful one; but he does not what the many do, but raises a city for Abderus, which we call after him, and a contest shall be ordained for Abderus, and there shall be contested over him boxing and pancratium and wrestling and all the games except those of horses.
AMPHIARAUS.

The chariot of two horses — for the four-horse car was not yet in the hands of the heroes, unless it were bold Hector's — carries Amphiaraus returning from Thebes, when the earth is said to have opened for him, that he might prophesy in Attica and tell true, wise among the all-wise. Of the seven who won the rule for Polyneices the Theban, none came home except Adrastus and Amphiaraus, but the Cadmean land held the rest. And the others perished by spears and stones and axes, but Capaneus is said to have been struck by the thunderbolt, having first, I think, in his boasting, struck at Zeus. These, however, belong to another tale; and the painting bids us look at Amphiaraus alone, fleeing into the earth with his very fillets and his very laurel. The horses are white, and the whirl of the wheels is full of haste, and the breath of the horses comes from the whole nostril; the ground is sprinkled with foam and the mane is blown sideways, and over them, drenched with sweat, lies a fine dust, making the horses less beautiful but more true. As for Amphiaraus, he is armed in all else, but neglects his helmet alone, baring his head to Apollo, and looks holy and oracular. The painter paints Oropus too as a youth among grey-eyed women, the sea-coast, that is; and he paints the place of meditation of Amphiaraus, a holy and sulphurous cleft. There too is Truth clad in white, there too the gate of dreams, for those who prophesy there have need of sleep; and Dream himself is painted in a relaxed form and wears white raiment over black — meaning, I think, his work by night and by day. And he holds a horn in his hands, as one bringing up dreams through the gate of truth.
STILL LIFE.

The hare in the little house is the catch of a net, and it sits on its haunches, moving its forefeet a little and lifting its ear, but it also looks with the whole of its gaze, and wishes to see behind it too, out of suspicion and its constant cowering; while the other, hung from the dry oak, its belly burst and slipped down through its feet, accuses the swiftness of the dog, who sits beneath the oak resting himself and showing that he alone made the catch. The ducks near the hare — count them ten — and the geese, as many as the ducks, you must not feel for fatness, for the part about the breast is all plucked, the fat there having the advantage in floating birds. And if you delight in leavened loaves or eight-piece loaves, those are near at hand in a deep basket; and if you want some relish, you have them themselves, for they share in fennel and parsley and besides in poppy, which is the seasoning of sleep. But if you long for a cooked dish, put that off to the cooks; do you eat the uncooked things. Why, then, do you not snatch the tree-ripened fruits, of which on each basket is this heap? Do you not know that a little later you will not meet such as these, but stripped already of their dew? And do not overlook the dessert, if you care at all for medlar and for chestnuts, which a most smooth plant rears in a sharp husk, strange to look at. Away with honey too, when this dried fig-cake is present, and, whatever you may call it, so sweet a confection. And native leaves wrap it round, giving the cake its bloom. I think the painting is bringing these gifts to the master of the farm, and he is bathing, perhaps, with an eye to Pramnian or Thasian wines, since it is possible to drink the sweet new must at the table, that, going down to town, he may smell of the wine-press and of freedom from cares, and may belch in the face of the town-loafers.
THE BOAR-HUNTERS.

Do not run past us, huntsmen, nor urge on your horses, before we have tracked out from you what you wish and what you are hunting. For you say you are rushing upon a wild boar, and I see the work of the beast: he has rooted up the olives and cut down the vines and has not left fig-tree or apple-tree or quince, but has torn everything out of the earth, some by digging, some by charging, some by rubbing against; and I see the beast himself bristling his mane and gazing fire, and his tusks rattle at you, my noble friends, for such beasts are dreadful in that they can be heard from very far through the din. I, however, think that, while you are hunting the bloom of that youth, you have been hunted by him, and are willing to face the danger first. For why are you so close? Why are you grazing him? Why have you turned toward him? Why do you crowd him with your horses? See what has happened to me: I have been carried away by the painting into thinking they are not painted, but are real and move and are in love; at any rate I jeer at them as if they could hear, and fancy I shall hear something in return — but you uttered nothing even to turn aside the madman, overcome like myself and unable to be checked from the deception and the sleep within it. Let us, then, consider what is painted, for we are standing before a painting. About the youth are gathered young men, handsome and of handsome pursuits, and as it were well-born; and one shows something of the wrestling-ground in his face, one of grace, one of wit, and one you would say had just lifted his head from a book. Horses carry them, alike yet no one like another — one white, one tawny, one black, one bay, silver-bridled and dappled and golden in their cheek-pieces. These colours, they say, the barbarians on the Ocean pour upon the bronze when it is red-hot, and they set and harden into stone and preserve what was painted. Nor do they agree in their clothing or attire, for one rides light-girt and nimble, a good javelin-thrower, I think, while another has fenced his breast, threatening some wrestling-match with the beast, and his legs are fenced too. But the youth rides on a white horse, whose head, as you see, is black, and a white circle is rounded off on the forehead, at the very fullness of the moon; and the horse has golden cheek-pieces and a bridle of Median scarlet, for this colour flashes upon the gold, like fiery stones. The youth's attire is a cloak with something of wind and billow in it. Its colour is from the Phoenician sea-purple, which the Phoenicians prize, and let it be loved most of sea-purples, for, though it seems to frown, it draws a certain bloom from the sun and is sprinkled as with the flower of the pomegranate. And out of modesty at being stripped before those present he is dressed in a sleeved scarlet tunic, and the tunic is measured to the half of the thigh and likewise of the elbow; and he smiles and looks bright-eyed and wears his hair long, only not so as to overshadow his eyes when the hair shall be disordered by the wind. Perhaps someone will praise his cheek too, and the proportions of his nose, and one by one the features in his face; but I admire him for his spirit, for he is strong as a huntsman, and is lifted up by his horse, and understands that he is loved. Mules and muleteers carry their gear for them — foot-traps and nets and hunting-spears and javelins and lances, on which are the barbs — and dog-leaders march with them, and watchers; and the breeds of the dogs are not only those good of nose or the swift among them, but also the brave, for there is need of strength too against the beast. He paints Locrian, Laconian, Indian, Cretan hounds, some high-spirited and baying, some thoughtful, which follow on and grin along the track; and as they go on they will sing to the Huntress, for there is a temple of hers there, and a statue smoothed by time, and heads of boars and of bears; and beasts let loose graze about her, fawns and wolves and hares, all tame and not fearing men. After the prayer they keep to the hunt. And the beast does not endure to lie hidden, but leaps out of the thicket, then falls upon the horsemen and at the first onset throws them into confusion, but is overcome by those who strike him — not having met a mortal blow, both because he fences against the strokes and because he is not struck by men full of courage, but, weakened by a superficial wound on the thigh, he flees through the wood, and a deep marsh receives him, and a lake by the marsh. So they pursue with shouting, the rest as far as the marsh, but the youth charges into the lake along with the beast, and these four hounds; and the beast rushes to wound the horse, but the youth, swerving aside from the horse and inclining to the right, throws with all his hand and strikes the boar just at the part that joins the shoulder-blade to the neck. Thereupon the dogs drag the boar to the land, while the lovers shout from the bank, as if vying with one another which shall out-shout his neighbour; and one has fallen from his horse, not having held on but having startled the horse, while another weaves a wreath for the youth from the meadow in the marsh. The youth is still in the lake, still in the posture in which he hurled the dart, while the others are struck with amazement and gaze at him, as if he had been painted.
THE BIRTH OF ATHENA.

The gods and goddesses are astounded — it having been said before that not even the Nymphs are absent from heaven, but are present to them with the rivers of which they are born — and they shudder at Athena, just now burst forth in armour from the head of Zeus by the contrivances of Hephaestus, as the axe shows. As for the material of the panoply, one could not infer it, for as many as are the colours of the rainbow shifting into now one, now another light, so many are those of the arms too; and Hephaestus seems at a loss by what means he may win the goddess, for his bait has been used up beforehand in that the arms sprang forth together with her. Zeus pants with pleasure, like those who have toiled out a great contest for great fruit, and beholds his daughter, proud of the birth; nor is there anything terrible of Hera here, but she rejoices, as if Athena had been born of her too. And already two peoples sacrifice to Athena upon two acropolises, the Athenians and the Rhodians, land and sea, the one with offerings without fire and unfinished, while the people at Athens have fire there, and the savour of victims, and the smoke is painted as it were fragrant and flowing up with the savour, whence the goddess came to them as to the wiser and those who sacrificed well; but to the Rhodians, it is said, gold flowed from heaven and filled their houses and their lanes, Zeus having broken a cloud upon them, because they too understood Athena. And upon the acropolis stands the spirit Wealth, painted winged, as from the clouds, and golden from the material in which he appeared. He is painted also seeing, for he came to them of forethought.
PERSEUS.

But this is not the Red Sea, nor are these Indians; rather they are Ethiopians, and a Greek man in Ethiopia. And as for the labour of the man, which he willingly endured out of love — you, my boy, I think, are not unacquainted with Perseus, who, they say, slew the Atlantic sea-monster in Ethiopia as it walked over the herds and the men of the land. This, then, the painter has praised, pitying Andromeda, that she was given up to the monster; the labour is already accomplished, and the monster is flung before the shore, flooded with springs of blood, by which the sea is red; but Love frees Andromeda from her bonds. He is painted winged, as is usual, but a youth, contrary to usage, and is painted panting and not far from having toiled. For Perseus, before the deed, offered up a prayer to Love that he should be present and fly down with him against the beast; and he came and heard the Greek. The maiden is pleasing, because she is white in Ethiopia, but more pleasing is her very form; she would surpass a dainty Lydian woman and a stately Attic and a sturdy Spartan. She has been beautified by the occasion, for she seems to disbelieve, and she rejoices amid her amazement and looks at Perseus, now sending him a kind of smile. He, not far from the maiden, lies on a sweet, frankincense-scented grass, dripping sweat into the earth and keeping the terror of the Gorgon hidden away, lest the people meeting it should turn to stone. Many cowherds are there, offering milk and wine to drink. The Ethiopians are pleasing in the strangeness of their colour, smiling grimly and not concealing their joy, and most of them are alike. Perseus welcomes these things too, but, propping himself upon his left elbow, he raises his chest, breathing hard with panting, looking at the maiden, and gives his cloak to the wind — a scarlet cloak, sprinkled with drops of blood which the beast breathed upon him in the contest. Let the descendants of Pelops be hale beside the shoulder of Perseus, for, beautiful and blood-flushed as it is, something of the toil has blossomed upon it, and the veins are swollen, which befalls them when the panting gets the upper hand. And much, too, he wins from the maiden.
THE LOOMS.

Since you sing of the web of Penelope, having met with a good painting, and it seems to you to have all the marks of a loom — the warp is sufficiently stretched, and flowers lie beneath the threads, and the shuttle all but utters a sound, and Penelope herself weeps with such tears as those with which Homer melts the snow — and she unweaves what she has woven, look too at the spider weaving close by, whether the painter has not woven in alongside both Penelope and the Seres still, whose threads are over-fine and scarcely visible. These are the gates of a house not faring well, and you will say it is widowed of masters, and within an empty court shows through, and not even the columns any longer prop it up, by reason of their sinking and falling, but it is inhabited by spiders alone, for the creature loves to weave in quiet. Look too at the spinnings: they spit out this thread and let it down to the floor, and the painter shows them coming down by it and climbing up again, "aloft in the air," as Hesiod says, and practising to fly; and they weave additional houses at the corners, some broad, some hollow — of these the broad ones are good for the summer, while those they weave hollow are good in winter. Beautiful, then, are these too of the painter; for to work out a spider so minutely, and to dapple it according to nature, and to paint its wool somewhat wretched and wild, belongs to a good and clever craftsman of the truth; and he has woven for us even its delicate parts. For lo: this square thread is set about the corners, like a cable of the web, and to the thread is tied a delicate web with many circles rounded off, and stretched meshes are woven from the first circle to the smallest, leaving between one another as much as the circles do. And the spinners walk through them, drawing tight the slackened threads. But they also win a wage for their weaving and feed on the flies whenever they are entangled in the webs; whence the painter has not passed over even their hunting, for one is held by the foot, one by the tip of the wing, one is eaten at the head, and they gasp, trying to escape; yet they do not disturb or break up the web.
PELOPS.

A soft robe, a fashion from Lydia, and a youth with the first down on his cheek, and Poseidon smiling on the youth and glorifying him with horses — these show that this is Pelops the Lydian, come to the sea to pray to Poseidon against Oenomaus, because Oenomaus will take no son-in-law, but, slaying the suitors of Hippodameia, prides himself on their spoils, hanging up their heads like those who have taken game. And to Pelops as he prays there comes a golden chariot out of the sea, and the horses are of the mainland and able to run across the Aegean with dry axle and light hoof. The labour, then, will run well for Pelops; but let us examine the labour of the painter. For it is no small contest, I think, to compose four horses and not to confuse the several legs of each, and to put spirit into them along with the bit, and to set one of them at rest in the very unwillingness to stand still, another in the wish to paw the ground, another in obedience; and one delights in the bloom of Pelops, and his nostrils are wide, as of one neighing. And this too is of the painter's wisdom: Poseidon is in love with the youth and brings him up to the cauldron and to Clotho, when Pelops seemed to flash from his shoulder; and from marrying he does not lead him away, since the youth has set his heart on it, but, content even to touch his hand, he has grown fast to the right hand of Pelops, suggesting to him the means for the race; while Pelops, now high-minded, breathes Alpheus too, and his brow is at one with the horses. He looks pleasant and lofty by reason of the high tiara nodding over him, from beneath which the youth's hair, like golden drippings, falls upon his forehead and matches it, and blooms together with the down on his cheek, and, shifting this way and that, stays in its fitting place. Of his haunch and breast, and whatever might be said of Pelops bare, the robe covers all to the very shin. For the Lydians and the other barbarians, shutting up their beauty in robes such as these, take their splendour from the weavings, when they might take their splendour from nature; and all the rest is hidden and within, but the part of the robe where the left shoulder is has been left undone by art, that its gleam might not be hidden, for night reigns and the youth gleams at the shoulder, as much as night gleams at the evening star.
ANTIGONE.

Those about Tydeus and Capaneus, and if there be any Hippomedon and Parthenopaeus here, the Athenians will bury, having undertaken the contest over the bodies; but Polyneices son of Oedipus, Antigone his sister buries by night, having gone forth from the wall, although it was proclaimed concerning him that he should not be buried, nor united to the earth which he was enslaving. In the plain, then, are corpses upon corpses, and horses as they fell, and the arms, as they slipped from the men, and this is the mire of gore, in which they say Enyo delights; and beneath the wall the bodies of the other captains are great and beyond the measure of men, while Capaneus is likened to a giant, for, besides his size, he has been struck by Zeus and is still smouldering. But Polyneices, great and like them, Antigone has lifted up, and will bury him beside the monument of Eteocles, thinking to reconcile the brothers, as much as is left. What shall we say, my boy, of the wisdom of the painting? For the moon casts a light not yet to be trusted by the eyes, and the maiden, full of amazement, has set herself to lament, embracing her brother with strong arms, yet she masters the lament, fearing, no doubt, the ears of the guards; and, wishing to gaze round at all about her, she nonetheless looks at her brother, bending her knee to the ground. The shoot of the pomegranate is self-grown, my boy, for the Furies are said to have planted it as a garden upon the tomb, and if you pluck of the fruit, blood is given forth even now. A marvel too is the fire upon the offerings to the dead, for it does not unite with itself, nor mingle its flame, but turns thence now one way, now another, and shows the unmingled nature of the tomb.
STILL LIFE.

It is good to gather figs too, and not to pass even these by in silence. Black figs dripping with juice are heaped on vine-leaves, and they are painted with the cracks in their skin, and some are gaping open, spitting out their honey, and some, by reason of their ripeness, are as it were split. Near them a branch is flung — not, by Zeus, bare or empty of fruit — and it shadows figs, some unripe and still green, some wrinkled and overripe, some half-split, showing the bloom of their juice, while on the tip of the branch a sparrow has pecked a hole in those which seem the sweetest of figs. The whole ground is strewn with nuts, of which some have rolled out of their husk, some lie in it, fast closed, some show the cleft between. But look too at pears upon pears, and apples upon apples, heaps and tens of them, all fragrant and gold-tinged. The redness in them you will not say is laid on, but has bloomed from within. And there are the gifts of the cherry, fruit such as this in clusters in a basket; and the basket is woven, not of foreign withes, but of the plant itself. And if you look at the binding of the vine-shoots, and the grape-clusters hanging from them, and how the grapes are one by one, you will sing, I know, of Dionysus, and "O lady, giver of clusters," you will say of the vine. You would say too that the grapes in the painting are good to eat and full of wine. And this too is most delightful: on fig-leaves green honey, already sunk into its comb, and ripe to overflow if one should press it, and a fresh cheese on another leaf, quivering, and bowls of milk not white only but glistening — for it seems to glisten by reason of the cream floating upon it.
EVADNE.

The pyre, and the things slaughtered into it, and the corpse laid upon the pyre, greater than one would think a man, and the woman lifting herself for so violent a leap into the fire — these things, my boy, are painted for the following reason. The kinsmen of Capaneus bury him at Argos; but he died at Thebes by the act of Zeus, having already mounted the wall. For you have somewhere heard from the poets that, having boasted somewhat against Zeus, he was struck with a thunderbolt and died before he fell to the ground, when the other captains too fell beneath the Cadmean wall. The Athenians having conquered, it is granted that they be buried; and Capaneus is laid out, having all else like Tydeus and Hippomedon and the rest, but this beyond all captains and kings: for Evadne his wife has set herself to die over him, neither drawing a sword to her throat nor hanging herself by any noose, such as women have chosen over their husbands, but she casts herself into the very fire, thinking she does not yet have her husband unless she have him too. Such, then, is the shroud of Capaneus; and the woman, like those who deck themselves with crowns and gold for the temples, that the offering may be made bright and to the favour of the gods, having so adorned herself and not looking pitiable, leaps into the fire, calling, I think, on her husband, for she seems to cry out, and she seems to me as if she would hold her head too beneath the thunderbolt on behalf of Capaneus. But the Loves, making these things their own, kindle the pyre from their little torches, and say the fire does not defile, but that they will use a sweeter and purer one, having buried with it those who used love well.
THEMISTOCLES.

A Greek among barbarians, a man among those who are not men, in very Attic fashion as to his cloak, declaims something wise, I think, transforming them and shifting them from their effeminacy. These are the Medes, and Babylon in the midst, and the royal sign, the golden eagle upon the shield, and the king upon the golden throne, dappled like a peacock. The painter does not deserve praise if he has well imitated a tiara and a calasiris or a kandys, or the monstrous shapes of beasts with which the barbarians embroider; but let him be praised for painting on the gold a man fine-spun and preserving what he has been forced to, and, by Zeus, for the appearance of the eunuchs; and let the court be golden, for it seems not to be painted but built, and we perceive the frankincense and myrrh, for the barbarians thus corrupt the freedom of the air; and let one spear-bearer converse with another about the Greek, astounded at him for a certain understanding of his great deeds. For you hear, I think, of Themistocles son of Neocles, that he came from Athens to Babylon after the divine victory of Salamis, at a loss where in Greece he should be safe, and conversed with the king about the things from which Xerxes had profited while he himself was general. Nothing of the Median scene astounds him, but he has taken courage, as one fixed upon the stone, and his voice is not in our native manner, Themistocles speaking Median, for he toiled this out there. And if you disbelieve, look at the listeners, how intelligently they signify with their eyes; look too at Themistocles, how the posture of his face is like those who speak, but the intent of his eyes has wandered through the use of speaking, since he learned anew.
PALAESTRA.

The place is the most beautiful of Arcadia, and that in which Zeus most delights — we call it Olympia — but there is not yet a prize of wrestling, nor a love of wrestling, but there will be. For Palaestra, daughter of Hermes, having now come of age in Arcadia, has invented wrestling, and the earth somehow rejoices in the invention, since the warlike iron will be laid up at truce among men, and stadiums will seem sweeter than camps, and they will contend naked. The wrestling-matches are children, for these high-spirited ones frolic about Palaestra, one over another, twisting themselves into her; and they would be earth-born, for the maiden says that, out of manliness, she would neither willingly marry anyone nor bear a child. And the wrestling-matches are kept apart from one another, for the grip joined with boxing is the strongest. As for the form of Palaestra, if it should be likened to a youth, she will be a maiden; but if it be taken as a maiden, she will seem a youth; for her hair is such as not even to be plaited, and her eye is of both characters, and her eyebrow such as to despise both lovers and wrestlers, for she says she is strong against both nations; and no one could touch her breasts even in wrestling, so much does she surpass in art. And the breasts themselves show a little of the impulse, as in a soft youth; and she praises nothing feminine, whence she does not even wish to be white-armed, nor does she seem to praise the Dryads, because they whiten themselves in the shade, but she asks colour of the Sun, since she dwells in hollow Arcadia, and he brings upon her, as it were, a kind of bloom and reddens the maiden with a moderate pomegranate-tint. To make the maiden sit, my boy, is something quite wise of the painter, for the shadows are most numerous for those sitting, and the sitting is sufficiently graceful for her; this is done too by the olive-shoot in her bare lap. And Palaestra, no doubt, welcomes this plant, since it aids wrestling and men greatly delight in it.
DODONA.

The golden dove still upon the oak, the wise one among oracles, and the prophecies which she utters from Zeus; and there lies this axe, which Hellus the woodcutter let fall, from whom the Helli at Dodona are named; and fillets are hung upon the oak, since, like the tripod at Pytho, it brings forth oracles. And one comes to ask it something, another to sacrifice, and this chorus from Thebes stands round the oak, making the wisdom of the tree their own; and the golden bird too, I think, was lured there. And the interpreters of Zeus, whom Homer knew as "with unwashed feet and sleeping on the ground," are men untaught and not yet furnished for living, and they say they would not even furnish themselves, for Zeus rejoices in them since they welcome the natural state; for these are priests, and one has charge of the roofing, one of the prayer, another must arrange the cakes, another the barley-grains and baskets, one sacrifices something, one will not let another flay the victim. And here are the Dodonian priestesses, of harsh and holy aspect, for they seem to breathe of incense and libations. And the place itself, my boy, is painted full of fragrance and full of prophetic utterance, and a bronze Echo is honoured in it, whom, I think, you see putting her hand to her mouth, since a bronze vessel was dedicated to Zeus at Dodona, sounding for much of the day and until someone took hold of it, not silent.
THE HOURS.

That the gates of heaven are in the keeping of the Hours, let us leave to Homer to know and hold, for it is likely that he conversed with the Hours when he was allotted the aether; but this, which the painting is intent upon, is easy for another too to make out. For the Hours, coming to the earth in their own forms and joining hands, wind round the year, I think, and the earth, being wise, bears for them in abundance all the things of the year. "Do not tread on the hyacinth or the rose," I will not say to the spring Hours, for by being trodden it appears sweeter and breathes something of the Hours themselves. "Do not step on the soft ploughlands," I will not say to the winter Hours among them, for to have them trodden by the Hours will make the corn-ear. These tawny ones tread upon the hair of the corn-ears, yet not so as to break or bend them, but they are so light that they do not even bow down the crop. "It is charming of you, vines, to wish to lay hold of the autumn Hours," for you love them, no doubt, because they make you beautiful and sweet-wined. These, then, are as it were the husbandry of the painting; but the Hours themselves are most delightful and of divine art. For what is their singing like, and what is the whirl of the circle, and that none of them appears behind us, because they all as it were come on — and the arm is up, and there is the freedom of unbound hair, and the cheek is warm from the running, and the eyes join the dance. Perhaps they grant something to be told in myth about the painter; for it seems to me that, meeting the Hours dancing, he was shaken by them into his art, the gods perhaps hinting that one must paint with beauty.
